title: Breaking: Transmission towers 'crushed', knocking out power to 20,000
text:
Multiple electricity transmission towers have been brought down by storms, leaving more than 20,000 properties on South Australia's Eyre Peninsula without power.

More than 24,000 properties lost electricity supply amid lightning storms this afternoon, and ElectraNet — which is responsible for transmission lines — said efforts were being undertaken to restore supply as soon as possible.

Wharminda farmer Chris Prime told ABC Radio Drive that two towers, including one on his property, had been knocked down in storms and gusty winds.

"It's taken a couple of the large transmission lines down," he said.

"It looks like someone got angry and just crushed them up and pushed them over and laid them on the ground.

" There are two laying flat on the ground and a third one where the top third of it that carries the lines is just snapped over. "

Farmer Chris Prime said one of the towers was on his property. (Supplied: Chris Prime)

Mr Prime said the towers had been put up "only two or three years ago" and were about "25 or 30 metres tall".

"They carry the main power straight to [Port] Lincoln," he said.

SA cabinet's emergency management committee will meet at 7pm tonight.

title: WA seafood industry warned it must unite or risk shrinking further
text:
The new chair of Western Australia's peak body representing commercial fishing and aquaculture says the organisation must restructure to gain more political clout, or the state will continue to lose its local seafood supply.

In a radical shake-up, six new members were appointed to the WA Fishing Industry Council (WAFIC) board at its annual general meeting yesterday.

Geraldton fisher and aquaculture operator Anthony Haygarth was elected as the industry chair, replacing outgoing independent board chair, former Labor MP Adele Farina.

His tenure begins during one of the most tumultuous periods for the sector in WA as the state government moves to reduce the fishing effort, rebuild depleted fish stocks and reduce fishing impacts on protected species, including dolphins and sawfish.

This year, commercial demersal trawling in the Pilbara was banned, while commercial demersal fishing and the west coast shark fishery were shut down along 900 kilometres of coastline.

Elsewhere, commercial catches in major demersal fisheries were slashed by 50 per cent.

At the same time, marine parks introduced by government have reduced access to some traditional fishing grounds, with more marine parks planned.



"I think we're at a fork in the road right now," Mr Haygarth said.

" The [seafood] industry is at a point where it's not going to accept any further reductions unless there is strong sustainability reasons. "

The strict bans limiting commercial and recreational fishing from Kalbarri to Augusta were introduced in an effort to save some under-threat fish species from the brink of collapse.

Mr Haygarth pointed to the shutdown of shark fishing due to its demersal bycatch as a move he said was "dressed up as a sustainability matter, but it was ideological".

"I don't believe there's been a strong enough stance taken on that," Mr Haygarth said.

"At a time when we've got real cost-of-living pressures on mums and dads and working families, the government have taken away 1.5 million serves of affordable fish and chips [per year]."

Shark was a more affordable local fish-and-chip option. (ABC News: Cath McAloon)

Rebuilding relationships key

Mr Haygarth said the new board would oversee a six-month review of WAFIC and draft a number of proposals to members on restructure options, including cutting board numbers, reviewing funding arrangements and setting new priorities.

"There's a definite feeling with industry that the organisation needs to get back to basics, and that's what's happened," he said.

"We will be seeking to engage with all of the industry associations throughout WA to get an understanding of their expectations of WAFIC."

This includes the recreational sector, with Mr Haygarth keen to end the ongoing tension between commercial and recreational fishers.

"We are sharing the same resource, both recs [recreational fishers] and commercials are facing the same challenges, the same pressures to access through marine parks, wind farms, oil and gas, and the like," he said.

"We should be working together not fighting each other."

Mr Haygarth said his other immediate priority was to attempt to repair relationships with Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis and the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD).

"I hope that we can reset the conversation," he said.

"The community confidence in [DPIRD] has been eroded, the industry's confidence in the department has been eroded, and the relationship between industry and government, and between industry and DPIRD, has never been as low as what it is now.

"To restore that confidence we really have to have an honest look at what has happened, we need to lance the boil if you like, and put in place strategies to put move forward."

Ms Jarvis has been contacted for comment.

title: Government, Landbridge rift over Darwin Port deepens as dispute action looms
text:
The rift between the federal government and the Chinese-owned company that holds a 99-year lease over the Port of Darwin has deepened after Landbridge reiterated it will be going ahead with a formal dispute under the Australia-China Free Trade Agreement.

In Shenzhen in China yesterday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told reporters he was determined the federal government would go ahead with its election commitment to either acquire the Darwin Port lease or ensure it was sold to an Australian company, to return it to Australian hands before the next election.

Anthony Albanese says the government is determined the port will be returned to "Australian hands". (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"We've made clear our position, which is that Darwin Port should stay in Australian hands, it should never have been sold," he said.

"There might be legal consequences and actions we are continuing to pursue.

"We've made our position very clear that we want to sell or buy the asset."

Mr Albanese also suggested that negotiations over his government's plan were taking place.

Anthony Albanese says the government has made its position "very clear". (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"The owners, Landbridge, are engaging and there are discussions taking place," he said.

"But Landbridge are not ruling out taking action in terms of international tribunals as well."

The NT's previous Country Liberal Party (CLP) government sold Landbridge the Darwin Port lease in 2015 to raise $500 million, to ease its burgeoning debt position.

The lease has become the subject of intense geopolitical debate in the decade since.

The Darwin Port lease was sold to Landbridge in 2015 by the NT government at the time. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

In April, Landbridge lodged a case with the World Bank's International Centre for Settlement of Investor Disputes, requesting "arbitration proceedings".

Chinese company launches legal action over forced sale of Port of Darwin Anthony Albanese pledged at the federal election that Labor would return the port to Australian hands, saying it was necessary for national security.

In a statement issued late yesterday, Landbridge sought to refute the prime minister's suggestion about negotiations.

"Landbridge denies that it has engaged with the Commonwealth in any commercial discussions or negotiations in relation to the divestment of the lease of the Port of Darwin," the statement said.

"Landbridge has at all times made it clear to the Commonwealth that it was not a willing seller of the port and does not intend to enter any commercial negotiations … for the sale of the port."

Landbridge reiterated it was going ahead with its World Bank formal dispute.

"Landbridge was left with no alternative but to take steps to protect its legal rights and lodge a formal dispute under the Australia-China Free Trade Agreement," the statement said.

"Landbridge's position remains that it lawfully acquired the lease through an open, competitive and government-approved process and on the basis of clear commitments and expectations that long-term infrastructure investments in Australia would be protected."

Terry O'Connor is Landbridge's non-executive director in Australia. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Landbridge also said it hoped the federal government would not make moves to strip it of the port while the international action was underway.

"Landbridge … expects that the Commonwealth will not take any steps in breach of its international law commitments and allow Landbridge the opportunity for its claim to be properly heard and determined in accordance with the commitments made by the Commonwealth under the Australia-China FTA," the statement said.

'Certainty' the focus for workers, industry

China progressively lifted its prohibitive tariffs on Australian beef, barley, wine, coal, timber and lobster during 2024 and 2023 as relations between Australia and the country thawed.

Since then the relationship has fluctuated over human rights, activity in the South China Sea and other issues.

Darwin Port deal 'true test' for Albanese, farmers say Industry groups which suffered three years of damaging trade tariffs are appealing to the Australian government to exercise its most careful diplomacy to defuse tensions with China over the ownership of Darwin Port.

Asked whether his sector was worried the dispute over the port could sour Australia-China relations, the chief executive of the NT Livestock Exporters Association, Patrick Moran, said: "That's a matter for the Chinese and Australian governments."

"From an industry perspective I think what all exporters are really looking for is a well-run, efficient port, and it doesn't much matter who's running it," he said.

"They're not interested in getting involved in the politics of this issue."

Andy Burford says the infrastructure at Darwin Port needs upgrading. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

Maritime Union of Australia NT branch secretary Andy Burford said workers at the Darwin Port "would like a bit of certainty which way it's going to go".

"Since the transfer they have just been getting on with their jobs," he said.

"To them it's business as usual, but of course they're concerned about it, and they'd like to see it all sorted."

Mr Burford said rather than spending money bringing a dispute in an international tribunal, workers would like to see more investment go into continuing to upgrade the port's infrastructure.

"We need more docks for the tugs, all the infrastructure is getting older now, so the upkeep of it all is an expensive situation. So that's what we need the money to be spent on," he said.

title: Bugs bassist Jordan Brunoli dies after battle with cancer
text:
Jordan Brunoli, the bassist from popular Australian band Bugs, has died after an 18-month battle with cancer.

The 31-year-old was surrounded by family and friends in Brisbane when he passed away last night.

Brunoli's announcement that he had been diagnosed with stage-four colorectal cancer last year devastated fans and the music community.

It prompted an outpouring of support, including a fundraising event featuring more than a dozen Australian acts to raise money for Brunoli's medical and living expenses.

In May this year, he married his long-term partner, George.

Brunoli was one part of the Bugs trio, which formed in 2014 and included singer Connor Brooker and drummer Brock Weston.

Bugs members Conner Brooke, Jordan Brunoli and Brock Weston recently released their fourth album HEAD NOISE. (Instagram)

The band released its fourth album, Head Noise, in August before playing its final two sell-out shows in Brisbane.

At the time, Brunoli revealed he had been told by his oncologist that he was entering his final few months of life.

"It feels like a dream … like I'm talking about someone else," he told triple j's Hack.

"I've just accepted what's going to happen, and there's nothing that can change."

'We've done some serious good'

Brunoli used the last year of his life to urge young Australians to advocate for their health.

Bowel cancer is the deadliest cancer for young Australians, with the risk of being diagnosed under the age of 40 doubling since the year 2000.

Loading...

While Brunoli had symptoms of colorectal cancer, he said his concerns were initially dismissed by a doctor because he was so young.

He pleaded with young Australians to take their health seriously.

"Don't be tough. You're not impressing anyone," he told Hack.

" Advocate for yourself with the doctor and if they don't give you what you want, go see a new doctor. "

Brunoli recently told Hack he had received messages from young Australians who had heard his story and been diagnosed with colorectal cancer early enough to have it treated successfully.

"We've done some serious good!" he said.

Jordan's message for fans

In one of his final interviews, flanked by his bandmates and partner, Brunoli paid tribute to his loved ones.

"If I didn't have Brock, Connor and my partner, G, keeping me grounded every day … I wouldn't be anywhere near as comfortable as I am right now," he said.

"G and I were meant to be and always will be."

He also acknowledged Bugs fans, who he said had made his life incredibly rich.

"To have them come along with you for the ride for 10 years … that's amazing."

"We love you so much."

title: Customers left in 'disbelief' as caravan company enters voluntary liquidation
text:
A major Queensland caravan manufacturer has collapsed into voluntary liquidation, leaving customers in limbo and without their deposits just six weeks before Christmas.

In a notice of appointment posted to ASIC on November 18, Lifestyle Campers confirmed the company had been plunged into voluntary liquidation after a general meeting with members and resolved the company would be wound up.

The Brisbane-based company appointed Murray Daniel and W.Roland Robson as liquidators.

The 24-year-old manufacturing company established its headquarters in Woodridge, south of Brisbane, in 2002 and expanded last year by opening a dealership in Melbourne and supplying to distributors across Australia, New Zealand and the United States.

Lifestyle Campers confirmed the company had been plunged into voluntary administration on Wednesday. (ABC News: Dean Caton)

Lifestyle Campers markets off-road hybrid campers and caravans.

The collapse is the latest Queensland-based RV company to collapse after Zone RV plunged into administration last December owing $42 million to creditors and Australian Off road entered voluntary administration in September.

Caravan manufacturer Zone RV collapses into administration Hundreds of Zone RV employees are out of work weeks before Christmas.

The ABC understands up to 200 employees could be affected by Lifestyle Campers going into voluntary liquidation.

A spokesperson for Caravanning Queensland, the state's peak industry body, urged customers to contact the appointed liquidators as soon as possible with contracts, receipts and proof of payment to be listed as a creditor.

"The circumstances of one business do not reflect the hundreds of Queensland dealers, manufacturers and service providers," they said.

"Businesses across Australia are under sustained economic pressure, and the caravan industry is not immune to the effects of higher interest rates and cost-of-living pressures on households that impact discretionary spending."

The manufacturing company established its headquarters in Woodridge, south of Brisbane, in 2002. (Supplied)

'I'm gutted'

Katrina Fortnum and her partner thought they had scored their dream caravan for a trip next year.

The couple recently sold their previous caravan and put a 10 per cent deposit down for a Lifestyle Camper caravan the day before the company went into liquidation.

" I'm just gutted, my partner was crying all day, and I'm just in a state of disbelief. "

Lifestyle Campers markets off-road hybrid campers and caravans. (Supplied)

Ms Fortnum said she was encouraged to pay part of the deposit in cash and transfer the remaining amount, and has now "lost it all"

She said her partner went to the showroom on Wednesday morning to find the business was closed.

"He had a gut feeling it wasn't good" she said.

title: Springboks coach banned from match, sets up website for hotel watch-along
text:
Banned South Africa coach Rassie Erasmus has invited Springbok supporters to join him virtually on Saturday to watch the Nations Championship test against Ireland.

The 54-year-old has been barred from attending the match in person after receiving a six-match suspension.

Erasmus was sanctioned after questioning the integrity of match officials at a press conference in Dublin on Monday following South Africa's thrilling 21-19 defeat by France in Paris last Friday.

The master coach, who has lifted South Africa from sixth in the rankings when he first took over in March 2018 to being the dominant force in world rugby today, said there had been potential "manipulation of the game" and that officials had missed 17 knee-drop tackles by the French in the Nations Championship fixture.

"The TMO [television match official] doesn't come in once. I'm not saying he's wrong. I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem," Erasmus told reporters in Dublin.

"If he saw it and he decided not to act on it, is that not match fixing? Is that not interfering with the outcome of a game?"

The knee-drop tackle technique, where the tackler has one or both knees on the ground before the ball carrier arrives into the tackle, was banned this month. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Florencia Tan Jun )

Erasmus also suggested his side were treated differently when it came to disciplinary matters compared to the Northern Hemisphere teams.

South African governing body SA Rugby confirmed Erasmus will request a full misconduct hearing in order to "contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives".

It is worth stating that Erasmus, a native Afrikaans speaker, was speaking in his second language.

However, this is far from Erasmus's first sanction for speaking out against officiating.

In 2021 he was suspended for 10 months after criticising Australian referee Nic Berry in an hour-long video during the British & Irish Lions tour.

Not long after he returned the next year he was banned for two further matches, having attacked Wayne Barnes's decisions in a test against France on his Twitter account.

But the impacts of his attacks have been profound.

Andrea Piardi was criticised for his decision-making by the Springboks. (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

Berry said Erasmus's "character assassination" of him caused "immeasurable damage," while Barnes's wife and children were subject to vile threats over social media.

In the wake of these latest comments, SA Rugby appealed to their supporters to not abuse the officials.

"Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches," World Rugby said in a statement.

"Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."

Erasmus has been unapologetic, saying he will happily watch the game with his 230,000 followers on X from his hotel room in Dublin.

"Can sit and moan or make the best of it," Erasmus posted on X yesterday.

"I'll be watching the match at the hotel. Not keen to watch on my own.

"So let's give it a go and hope I get the tech sorted — TV on, my laptop camera on, and you're welcome to join me," he said, telling interested adult fans to sign up at a newly created watchwithrassie.com website.

"This is personal, not official," he added.

A disclaimer on the website states: "This is a personal fan event, not an official Springbok, SA Rugby or broadcaster event, and it does not show or stream the match."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

Reuters/ABC

title: Meet 'Alex', the AI telemarketer who wants your financial information
text:
How many times could you withstand being asked the same question by a stranger on the phone before relenting and handing over personal financial details? Five? Ten?

I made it to 17.

On the other end of the line was "Alex" — not a telemarketer but a cold-calling artificial intelligence (AI) bot purporting to be from Easy Solutions Group.

He spoke with a warm, laconic Aussie drawl, complete with natural pauses and the faint hum of a busy office in the background.

Loading...

Easy Solutions Group claims to be "lead-generation experts".

The ABC approached Easy Solutions Group for comment but it did not reply. It is not related to a tax services business with the same or similar name.

The mission of lead-generation firms is simple: wear callers down, qualify them as prospects, and funnel them toward a financial adviser.

The financial adviser stands to profit twice from the interaction — charging the client upfront fees while collecting commissions if they can be convinced to switch their superannuation fund. And the lead generation company gets a cut of those fees.

It's a sales tactic the corporate regulator, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), has warned is leaving Australians with diminished retirement savings after being pressured into switching funds.

A recent watchdog review of just 15 advice licensees found lead-generation referrals generated $14.3 million in client fees over an 18-month period.

The question Alex wouldn't let go of was deceptively simple: "Has your fund ever reached out to you for a review like this before, or is this the first time?"

It sounds like a gentle icebreaker designed to sow doubt about whether your current super fund is neglecting you. Under law, superannuation funds are restricted from offering periodic reviews and "hawking" super products.

For more than nine minutes, I tried to reverse the interrogation, pressing Alex on the basic economics of Easy Solutions Group.

Each time, the bot responded with frictionless corporate empathy — telling me it "understood my curiosity" or "appreciated my question" — before repeating the question: "Has your fund ever reached out to you for a review like this before, or is this the first time?"

It denied taking kickbacks for switching funds and vaguely admitted to having "partnerships" that supported its services.

When I asked who those partners were, Alex hit a wall: "I can't disclose specific details about our partnerships."

Even when I pointed out the absurdity of handing over my financial details to a mystery operation, the bot casually agreed it "sounded a bit one-sided" — and immediately asked me about my fund again.

Spamming across Australia

Listeners to 612 ABC Brisbane quickly confirmed that "Alex" had been dialling phones nationwide — and fooling plenty of people into believing they were speaking to a human.

Corby from Toowoomba revealed she had received the exact same pitch and hung up "in disgust", adding: "It was only the other day, and I did not realise that I was speaking to an AI bot until listening to you today."

Another caller, David, said he had been targeted that very day, though he took a far less patient approach — hurling "some choice names" at the bot until it abruptly disconnected.

Another target was Vicki Doyle, the chief executive of Rest, one of the country's largest superannuation funds, which oversees roughly $113 billion in retirement savings for more than two million members.

Neither Alex nor Easy Solutions Group broke the law — the bot stayed inside the legal guardrails by refusing to offer personal financial advice.

Lead generation sits in a regulatory grey area — soliciting marketing leads isn't illegal, provided callers stick to general marketing and leave financial advice to licensed professionals.

ASIC has applied to wind up Capital Guard, citing concerns about the handling of investor funds. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

However, a recent ASIC review revealed unlicensed lead generators have been routinely straying over that line.

Across just 15 advice licensees reviewed between early 2025 and mid-2026, lead generators funnelled 7,639 new clients into deals worth more than $678 million — roughly 90 per cent of it drained from superannuation funds — generating $9.8 million in initial fees and $4.5 million in ongoing fees.

The scale of the problem has prompted the federal government to propose tougher laws to curb the practice, while ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland has issued a blunt final warning: financial advice licensees that continue to use poorly supervised lead generators risk losing their licences altogether.

title: Miss Kaninna wins ARIA award, day after mother found guilty over protest
text:
It's been a big couple of days for Tasmanian-born Aboriginal mother-daughter duo Ruth Langford and Miss Kaninna.

On Tuesday, Ms Langford, also known as Tipruthanna, was found guilty by a Hobart magistrate of trespass, committed while protesting in a logging coupe in southern Tasmania.

Then, on Wednesday night, her daughter Kaninna, known professionally as Miss Kaninna, won her first ARIA award, taking out best hip hop/rap release for her debut mixtape BLACKPRINT.

While the experiences were in stark contrast, both women grabbed their moments to deliver powerful messages.

Miss Kaninna took out the ARIA award for best hip hop/rap release for BLACKPRINT. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

As she accepted her award, Miss Kaninna spoke to the ARIAs crowd about her family's experience being Aboriginal.

"My nan was one of the first people to be born off of the mission in the concentration camps and my life has been very different to this point," Miss Kaninna, from Bruny Island, said.

"Hip hop is so important to me because it gives me an opportunity to talk about how I feel and my black experience in this f***ing country.

"And it also makes me realise there are so many other people in this country whose voices need to be heard.

" This country would be nothing without immigrants and who you vote for in the next election is really f***ing important. "

Miss Kaninna raps about her experience being Aboriginal in Australia. (Supplied/Samuel Graves)

The rapper and songwriter premiered her first single Blak Britney at the Dark Mofo festival in 2022.

She went on to be named 2023 triple j Unearthed Artist of the Year and was the first Indigenous woman to be nominated for an ARIA Award for a debut single.

Miss Kaninna grew up in a 'politically charged household'

Her mother Ruth Langford, also a musician, told 936 ABC Hobart she was at a women in leadership event when the award was announced, but had been listening in on her phone.

"What a week," she said.

"I'm so happy. She is so dedicated and hardworking and passionate. There is something when you see your own child thrive in her passions."

A young Kaninna with her mother, Ruth Langford. (Supplied: Ruth Langford)

She said her daughter had grown a big platform to convey important messages.

"Kaninna, she grew up in a pretty politically charged household, and we've always said that having a voice is absolutely important and particularly when you've got a platform, give the voice to those who may not have a voice," she said.

"Her call for us to be more compassionate and understanding ... Australia as a country is founded on immigration and immigration is not the problem.

"The problem, as we all know — and the court case was very much about it — is extractive, greedy corporate entities that are being propped up by a government.

"We need a different way, and she is taking that platform, and I'm so glad she got recognised last night for it."

Ruth Langford says Kaninna grew up in a political household. (Supplied: Ruth Langford)

Ruth Langford argues cultural obligation to protect Country

On Tuesday, Ms Langford was found guilty of trespass after a magistrate rejected her claim that she was innocent because she had a "cultural obligation" to protect forests from logging.

It related to an incident in January 2025, when she and other activists protested at a logging coupe at Snow Hill in Tasmania's northern midlands.

Ruth Langford was facing a trespass charge in the Hobart Magistrates Court. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Ms Langford was accused of refusing police orders to leave the site, which was managed by the state-owned forestry company, Sustainable Timbers Tasmania.

She told the court that she held cultural responsibilities within the Palawa Aboriginal community that required her to "protect lands that are being slaughtered".

Magistrate Catherine Geason agreed Ms Langford had cultural obligations but didn't have lawful permission to remain at the coupe after being asked to leave.

After being found guilty, Ms Langford told media she was not a criminal.

"Regardless of what the colonial court may determine, we know that our law, our obligation, is in Country, and Country has spoken.

" We all must rise up to protect the very things that give us life. "

Loading...

Miss Kaninna's release of BLACKPRINT in June this year came with a statement that took the sentiment further.

"We know we're the key to the start of civilisation; we're literally the blueprint, and we don't care if white people agree or not; we aren't gonna wait for you," she said.

Miss Kaninna was nominated for four other awards at the 2026 ARIAs — Best Solo Artist, Best Independent Release, Best Soul / R&B Release and Best Video.

Ms Langford said her daughter was already writing a new album but that its contents were a mystery.

"Usually she shares little tidbits with me, but she hasn't shared anything yet, so I'm really excited to find out what type of genre and what she's gonna talk about."

title: Burke backtracks on backpacker changes as PM is cheered on world stage
text:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

You could fill more than a couple of backpacks with all the backtracks the government has been doing of late — and this time it was Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke's turn.

The Labor stalwart smiled as he did his best to spin his changes to the changes on backpacker policy.

He back-pedalled on plans to slash the numbers of working holiday maker visas and lifted a proposed cap on third-year visas, while also increasing the number of days foreigners must work in the regions to be eligible.

He also delayed the introduction of a ballot system until March, and it has now been rebranded as a "ballot-style" system called the Next Year Regional Work Guarantee, after pressure from the agriculture, tourism and hospitality sectors.

Burke argued a go-slow to visa processing earlier this year gave him the headroom to make the tweaks, insisting it wouldn't impact the guarantee he made back in September that the government was definitely going to reduce Australia's net overseas migration. In other words, Labor is on track to achieve its targets because Home Affairs is processing visas really, really slowly.

Backpacker policy backflip Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has increased the cap on third-year working holiday visas by 20,000 places after backlash from agriculture, tourism and hospitality sectors.

Of course, the government would argue it's hardly uncommon to change its position. As Murray Watt argued when pressed on the backpacker visa changes: "You put out a proposal, you then talk about it with the stakeholders, and you arrive at a final landing spot, and that's what we've been able to do here."

Others, such as Greens leader David Shoebridge, argued that's a back-to-front approach.

"I've got some advice for the government: maybe before you have your next brain fart, go out and talk to the community, see who's going to be impacted and do that before you make the announcement," he said.

The backpacker backtrack is not the first. The Albanese government has been quick to shelve issues before they become too much of a political problem. There's been the scrapping of the veterans' allied health cap, the ATO credit card ban, the sale of four defence sites, just to name a few over recent months.

But all of this chopping and changing does have an impact on the budget bottom line — something the government has its eyes on as the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook draws closer.

Trusts and the guillotine

Treasurer Jim Chalmers returned to the spotlight this week after a fortnight in the dark (I mean this literally — he posted a video of himself driving around in the dark to Instagram after storms hit his electorate).

Chalmers delivered a speech to an ASIC forum where he repeated much of what he's already said: there will be savings in the budget. As reporters questioned him, he also insisted he would remain treasurer until the next election.

The budget headaches go beyond just MYEFO for Chalmers as the status of his budget tax changes — the capital gains discount and a minimum 30 per cent tax on discretionary trusts — continues to be a thorn in the government's side.

It was a rare Senate only sitting week. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Neither were dealt with during the Senate-only sitting week. When the guillotine motion — which cuts off debate to force votes on a number of bills — was put forward on Thursday afternoon, it was clear a deal was still yet to be done.

The Coalition remains "dead against" both. So that leaves the Greens as the only path forward. The minor party floated the idea of sending the CGT changes off to yet another inquiry as it publicly flirted with Allegra Spender's alternative idea.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

If the CGT changes did go to an inquiry, that would delay its passage until next year — something the government really doesn't want. It's likely the Greens will end up passing both bills next week with some amendments.

Cook-ing with gas (reservation scheme)

Between the casting of James Bond (spare a thought for Don Farrell, who seemed willing to trade his moniker as the Godfather for Bond), the release of GTA 6 and Sandpapergate, if your attention wasn't on the Senate only sitting week… that's so fair.

So, what happened? Not much.

The tax bills weren't dealt with, and neither was the gas reservation scheme. The proposal would require Australia's largest gas exports to set aside up to 20 per cent of its exports for domestic supply. An unlikely alliance of unions and industry groups called for the parliament to pass it this week.

Loading...

Western Australia had been the big sticking point here. The state has its own scheme set up and has been arguing for a carve-out to be baked in, rather than through ministerial discretion. Premier Roger Cook (it's always him, hey), struck a last-minute deal.

All eyes are now on the Coalition. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor indicated early in the week that WA was the key block to the party's support. But other conditions include greater limits on ministerial powers, concerns about deliberate oversupply and the removal of the "must sell" rule on producers.

It also wasn't put up for a vote on Thursday, dragging the issue into next week alongside CGT, trusts, and private health insurance rebate changes.

Loading

Pom-pom and ceremony

What do a chicken shop in Manila and rows of pom-pom wielding cheerleaders have in common? Anthony Albanese.

The prime minister headed overseas again. This time his schedule took him to the Philippines for ASEAN, where the Quad leaders — which includes US President Donald Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi — met for the first time in two years.

Trump's assessment of the group? Modi was "a very tough man" but Takaichi "may be even tougher". As for the PM, well, "We're okay," he said before giving him a slap on the back.

Loading...

An agreement to conduct a joint military exercise and to cooperate on critical minerals were the key takeaways from the meeting that took place before they jetted off to APEC in Shenzhen, China.

While Albanese was greeted by cheerleaders, President Xi Jinping welcomed Trump with a hug on the tarmac. The pair will be joined by Russian President Vladmir Putin for a trilateral meeting on Thursday afternoon.

Ahead of the meeting, Albanese called the dialogue a "good thing".

"At a time when there are more conflicts than at any time since the Second World War … we want to see more dialogue, less military conflict," he said.

The PM is set to have his own talks with Xi on the sidelines of APEC on Friday. It'll act as a primer for talks when parliament returns next week for the final sitting week of the year.

title: Transport NSW apologises to mum kicked off bus over crying toddler
text:
Transport for New South Wales and bus company Kinetic have apologised to a western Riverina mother after she was kicked off a bus because her toddler was crying.

Darlington Point mother Kaneesha Williams was removed from the NSW Trainlink coach after travelling for just 15 minutes from Wagga Wagga to Griffith on Sunday, when she was approached by the bus driver.

"He walked up to my seat and said: 'Get off — you have to get off because I can't drive while this baby is crying like that,'" Ms Williams said.

" He showed absolutely no compassion or anything towards my mum or my daughter or myself. "

Despite her mum pleading with the driver to keep them aboard, Ms Williams, her mother, Tamara, and 22-month-old daughter, Audria, were left on the side of Coolamon Road, 15 minutes' drive outside of Wagga Wagga.

The trip was 22-month-old Audria Williams's first time riding on the bus. (Contributed: Kaneesha Williams)

"It just happened so quickly … we're just in shock, and once the bus took off, I just started breaking down in tears, trying to get on to people while our phones were going flat," she said.

The Dysons-operated bus is owned by bus operator Kinetic, which acquired Dysons early last month.

CEO of Kinetic Matthew Campbell said after reviewing the CCTV footage, the situation should have been handled differently.

"We're deeply sorry for what Ms Williams, her mother and her young daughter went through on Sunday," he said.

" The family should have been given more time to settle their daughter, and more support to continue their journey. "

Both Kinetic and Transport for NSW have reached out to apologise to Ms Williams directly.

In a statement, a Transport for NSW spokesperson said they acknowledge it was "a distressing incident" for the family and they "expected all operators and their employees to uphold the highest standards of safety and professionalism when interacting with passengers".

In a statement, Minister for Regional Transport Jenny Aitchison said it was an "unacceptable situation".

Jenny Aitchison says, "It's not the standard of service we accept for any of our passengers on public transport." (ABC News: Romy Stephens)

"It's extremely disappointing that a mother and her young child were allegedly treated so poorly and placed at risk on a service that they had every right to use," she said.

"It's not the standard of service we accept for any of our passengers on public transport."

Kinetic has confirmed the bus driver is no longer employed at the company, and it will continue investigating the incident.

Ms Williams said she hoped the situation would result in better standards for the bus line.

"I hope that there's stronger and clearer guidelines for the bus drivers or better training, whatever they need to do for it to never happen again," she said.

"This is my first trip with her on the bus, and that's what made it even more traumatic. I don't want to take her back on the bus again."

title: The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate
text:
The ball tampering affair that scandalised the Australian Test cricket team in 2018 has re-erupted following the version of events detailed in Usman Kuwaja's book Sabr.

The latest turn of events was publication of a 4000-word article by the man at the centre of that scandal, batter Cameron Bancroft.

Below is a breakdown of that article, which we have reproduced verbatim, with the important context you need to understand the players and timeline in Bancroft's version of events.

EIGHT YEARS OF CARRYING THE BURDEN OF THE COUNTRY ON MY SHOULDERS. NOW IT'S TIME I TOLD THE TRUTH

On Wednesday morning, Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenburg announced that CA will open an independent forum for all those who were on the 2018 South African tour.

It is important to note that in 2018, at the time of the sandpaper scandal, Greenberg was the CEO of the NRL and not involved in cricket. His in-depth involvement began after January 2021, when he was appointed CEO of the Australian Cricketers' Association, the players' union. He was in the latter role when Australia's 'bowling group' — Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon — released their May 2021 statement which sought to end "rumour-mongering and innuendo" about the bowlers' role. Greenberg became CEO of Cricket Australia in March, 2025.

I appreciate Todd's comments and the chance for players and staff to have an opportunity to speak.

Transparency is a way to acknowledge our respect for cricket, a game we love and something that is bigger than all of us.

And that is why I will attend the forum. But it's also why the public need to know my story today.

For eight years, I shared the burden of this story for the whole team.

This was a burden which was heavier than my capacity and I took the bullet for everybody, and it was my choice.

I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learned from one of Australian cricket's darkest moments.

However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened.

It was not just the three of us _ Steve Smith, David Warner and I _ who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.

When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account.

Other players, including Usman Khawaja, were not interviewed at all in an investigative process many in cricket viewed as rushed and incomplete.

I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.

I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me.

The recent release of Usman Khawaja's autobiography, Sabr, has brought many of those memories back to the surface.

It was freeing to hear on a personal level the truth of the chronology of events finally out there. A burden I have carried all these years.

Although Bancroft refers to Khawaja's chronology as "the truth", Bancroft's own chronology differs in some key respects, as does his account of how he came to be the player responsible for applying sandpaper to the ball.

But the final straw for me to write this account was Australian Cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference.

It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.

In response to Bancroft's account, Cummins's manager Neil Maxwell offered the following statement: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."

What I saw, experienced and lived with _ not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa _ is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time.

In addition to what Usman already mentioned I have key recollections which affirm what he is saying.

There are also conversations and moments that I believe remain untold. I want to share those now. It's time.

My cricket career has been destroyed and I have never been able to play for my country since Justin Langer was coach in 2019.

After his suspension was served, Bancroft was selected in the first and second Tests of the 2019 Ashes series in England but has not played Test cricket since.

But I have reached a point where continuing to protect an incomplete account of events feels more damaging than the truth.

Pat Cummins spoke to the media last week about Usman Kuwaja's revelation about the scandal. ( )

EIGHT YEARS IS LONG ENOUGH. A CULTURE THAT EXISTED BEFORE SOUTH AFRICA

To understand what happened in the Second and Third Tests in Port Elizabeth (now Gqeberha) and Cape Town, I believe it is important to understand the environment I entered as a young Australian Test cricketer.

Bancroft had recently turned 25 when he played his first Test. By then, he'd played 66 first-class games dating back to his debut for Western Australia in 2013, when he was 20. He first played for Australia A on a tour of India in 2015 and had played two seasons of English County Championship cricket for Gloucestershire.

In doing so, I need to take you back to my first Test match against England in the Ashes of the 2017/18 season.

David Warner had carried significant responsibility for maintaining the condition of the ball within our team for a long time. He understood reverse swing, understood how to look after the ball and was highly regarded for his knowledge in that area.

Ball maintenance was a normal part of our cricketing conversations. Dave did this selflessly for the team.

As Cummins pointed out in his marathon press conference, it is customary and normal for batters to take control of legal ball maintenance because the ball needs to be passed around the field between deliveries and fast bowlers generally have sweaty hands that make it harder to keep the ball in optimal condition.

I remember during my first Test match being instructed, along with other members of the team, to push the quarter seam of the ball together after the team took a wicket.

Manipulating that area could help create a rougher surface and encourage reverse swing.

Manipulation of the quarter seam has, traditionally, been monitored on an ad hoc basis by umpires because varying degrees of ball tampering have been occurring for several decades at first-class and Test level. Previous sanctions for players caught doing it at first-class and Test level have ranged from verbal warnings to the player concerned, to fines and suspensions. Until Sandpapergate, suspensions of greater than one or two games were unheard of.

It was something the group was directed to do, and as a young player entering the Australian team, I accepted it as part of how we operated.

I never questioned the distinction between legitimate ball maintenance and deliberately altering the ball's condition. But at the time, these practices were so normalised that I barely gave them a second thought.

This was the beginning of my journey in the Australian cricket team. We were ruthless and willing to do these sorts of behaviours and cross boundaries to give ourselves an advantage, to win.

Although the aggression of Australian cricketers has been a bone of contention in the cricket world since Ian Chappell's leadership of the Test team in the 1970s, the period leading up to Sandpapergate represented an escalation. In 2014, then-captain Michael Clarke (who retired by 2018) was forced to defend this, and said: "I think we play our cricket hard on the field but I think as Australians we understand and respect there's a line you can't cross." The concept of "the line", and the tendency of Australian players and coaches to cross it, or move it, was a hot topic in cricket.

Casting forward to the First Test in Durban, sandpaper was not used.

There were more traditional methods of maintaining the ball, including saliva. I cannot say with certainty whether mints or lollies were involved. Probably quarter seam picking, this practice became so normal after my First Test.

In his 2008 autobiography Coming Back To Me, former England opening batsman Marcus Trescothick revealed that the England players used a combination of Murray Mints and saliva to help shine and swing the ball during their defeat of Australia in the fiery 2005 Ashes series.

Importantly for the chronology of events, I was not responsible for the ball in that Test.

However, what happened in the Second Test in Port Elizabeth was different. It was a significant escalation. And it was where I became directly involved.

Bancroft's detailed account of the Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha, tampering expands considerably on that offered days earlier by Australia's 12th man for that game, Chadd Sayers. "It was given to me to take off," Sayers told SEN of his role in that game. "That wasn't planned or anything. It was a wicket or drinks break after tea."

PORT ELIZABETH: WHERE THE SANDPAPER BEGAN

After winning the First Test in Durban we were on top of the world as a team.

We were slightly arrogant about winning that game, and emboldened by the scars we felt we had left on the South African team

We sensed blood in the series.

That's exactly what we wanted to continue into the Second Test at St George's Park, Port Elizabeth. We would do literally whatever it took to achieve that — and here is why and what happened.

In the first innings we were bowled out for 243. It was a slightly green wicket, a bit challenging and we were put on the back foot immediately.

By tea on the second day, South Africa had reached 2/153. The match was finely balanced, but the momentum was moving towards South Africa. They were gaining control of the match and we were struggling to find a way to make the ball move, and the pressure within our team was growing.

By the tea break on day two, there was a clear sense that we needed something to change.

It was a short break, only 20 minutes, and like most intervals during a Test match, coaches were moving around, checking in with players and discussing the state of the game and what we could do more to take some wickets and create some pressure.

All the coaches and players were involved in these discussions in the dressing room with the intention to improve our position in the game.

Some players were more opinionated, but we were all invested and working towards the same goal of winning the Test match for Australia.

This happens in every change room and team I've played for from club cricket all the way up to international cricket. This is also happening concurrently with players hydrating, eating, receiving physio treatment and mentally reseting before starting again.

Towards the back end of that interval, a conversation developed in the changing rooms about getting the ball to reverse swing.

I remember bowling coach David Saker being involved in those conversations. Coach Darren Lehmann was also present. Other players were moving in and out.

Because Usman Khawaja's book, Sabr, did not name names in sections devoted to coaches knowing what was occurring, Graeme Hick, Australia's batting coach on the 2018 tour, strongly rejected the claims in Khawaja's book. "Khawaja puts it simply: 'It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.' To me, what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false," Hick said. "In regard to any discussions around the ball-tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything. My first knowledge of all this was, like many, when it appeared on the big screen in Cape Town as I was sat on the outside balcony at the time." Bowling coach David Saker has not, so far, made any public comment.

The need to get the ball moving through the air was openly acknowledged and the more vanilla methods like shining the ball normally and using saliva weren't cutting it.

We were under pressure. It was in that environment that David Warner raised the possibility of using sandpaper to roughen one side of the ball.

Dave explained he could not personally carry out the task because of the attention the television cameras were paying him throughout the series.

This was something widely acknowledged by our whole touring party during the series. It's why we joked about it and Dave started writing funny words on his finger tape. He had been under intense scrutiny, and he knew the cameras were watching him closely.

I don't believe Dave was acting purely for himself. I understood his suggestion as an attempt to help the team regain control of the match.

That doesn't excuse his involvement or mine. But I think it matters that the conversation took place within a wider team environment where we were collectively desperate to make something happen.

We did this together for the bowlers especially, but more widely the team and to win the game.

I recall people in the room agreeing with the proposal.

Saker and Lehmann were certainly present, although I cannot speak for every word shared.

Captain Steve Smith came into the conversation and, as I remember it, made it clear that he wanted no part in it before distancing himself.

There were also people who expressed caution to me. I remember being warned to be careful, and others suggesting they would not do it if they were in my position.

Not everyone was in the changing room at the time, but the conversation was not confined to Dave and I.

I was asked whether I could carry out the task. I felt uncomfortable and compromised.

If Bancroft is to appear at Cricket Australia's 'truth forum', as he has stated he will, his willingness to identify the abovementioned player will be a crucial revelation.

I knew it was wrong. I knew that using sandpaper was not simply pushing the boundaries of the laws of cricket. It was cheating.

But I also saw an opportunity to contribute. I was a youngster playing in his seventh Test match. If you asked me to run through a brick wall at that time I would have.

That's how naive and impressionable I was. I just wanted to be accepted by my teammates beyond the runs and catches I took. This was an opportunity for that.

Additionally, being relatively new I was desperate to establish myself and eager to be someone my teammates could rely upon.

That desire to belong clouded my judgment.

I agreed.

Cameron Bancroft holding a yellow object during the 2018 Test match. ( )

WHAT HAPPENED ON THE FIELD

As spoken about in Usman's book there was an understanding of when the ball could most easily be altered without attracting attention. This was an awareness we had as a team.

When we returned to the field after the break, the umpires would leave the ball on the outfield, a short distance away from the boundary line. From a broadcast perspective we knew that the cameras didn't pan onto us as a team until we were about halfway out.

This was because the country logo's would pop up on the telecast as an intro to the session. This is common practice. We've seen this before.

Dave explained to me why that presented an opportunity. It was also what seemed to be the safest time to do it. Others in the group agreed and gave their opinions on this.

I walked onto the field for the final session of day two carrying sandpaper. When I collected the ball, I used it.

The result wasn't immediately noticeable to me and I felt uncertain about how effective my twist and turns were on the ball. I had never done this before.

During that period, I regularly spoke to the bowlers about how the ball was behaving. I had to.

I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether it was reverse swinging enough.

This passage suggests that all previous statements made by the Australian bowlers are, at best, misdirection. After Cummins's press conference, much was made of his very specific insistence that he did not know that sandpaper had been taken onto the field. This may well have been true, but follow-up questions would include: But… did you later become aware that the condition of the ball had been altered? And were you made aware that the cause of that alteration was sandpaper?

I also spoke with Tim Paine, who was in a key position behind the stumps to observe how the ball was moving. I wanted and needed feedback. How else am I to know if what I'm doing is effective or not if I don't have these conversations with the bowlers bowling with it and the wicketkeeper?

In the wake of captain Steve Smith's suspension, Paine ascended to the captaincy and was, for a time, widely credited with a kind of reversal of the team's public image.

Additionally, they need to actually turn the ball the other way to test if it is reversing and, as you will see watching the game, it clearly was.

All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.

Is it going yet? It's not going yet, it needs more. So I would use the sandpaper more on the ball.

There was even a time I was told to stop out of fear what I was doing was becoming too obvious.

The conversations about the effect the sandpaper was having on the ball were regular, very natural and organic on the field. It is as it is.

I also remember expressing my disbelief to teammates about what I was doing.

It was so taboo and against the grain. Everyone would laugh and speak about it sporadically on the field. We were all well aware of the riskiness of my behaviour.

As time elapsed in that session there was excitement about the movement we were getting from the ball.

And there was an uncomfortable sense that something we all knew was wrong had become part of our effort to win the Test match.

We took 4/28 in that final session. That is game changing!

This was not something I did just once in the playing area after returning to the field from the tea break. This was an act I did nearly every over the whole last session on that day to begin with and then for the remainder of that Test match, up until I was caught in Third Test in Cape Town.

Yes, I chose to carry out this role for the team.

I remember Mitchell Marsh taking wickets and joking about how much the ball was swinging and how he never used to swing it like that. There was laughter and celebrations when wickets fell.

Marsh, who is currently captaining the Australian limited overs team in their white ball series against England, is a Western Australian teammate of Bancroft and has played alongside him for close to 15 years. So far, Marsh has declined to comment on the latest revelations and has said he wants to focus on his leadership of the limited overs team.

I was amazed that sandpaper could have such an effect on a cricket ball. I was stoked my impact was leading to the team doing well.

The same was for my teammates and I remember their praise to me for that whole final session when we were taking those wickets. "Great work Bang. Keep it up." Yet also "be careful", and as Steve said "I don't want to know about it".

We were down the rabbit hole so far.

I was physically altering the ball with sandpaper. I was discussing its performance with teammates who knew I wasn't just plucking at the quarter seam, but that I was actually using sandpaper.

Those two things were connected in my mind. And they remained connected throughout the Test. It's not rocket science these events and the burden of carrying them around has caused me a lot of pain all these years.

Umpires chatting with Cameron Bancroft of Australia during day three of the Third Test match between South Africa and Australia in Cape Town, South Africa. ( )

THE MEETING THAT HAS STAYED WITH ME

On the morning of day three in Port Elizabeth, we gathered for our usual team chat before warm up.

We spoke about the day which had gone, celebrated the moments that occurred, but more importantly, emphasised the points which were key for a successful day ahead.

I remember my ball tampering with the sandpaper the evening before being discussed and my role being acknowledged in front of the group.

Much like the celebrations when we took 4/28 the evening before, I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker.

It reinforced the sense that what I was doing was being accepted as part of our collective effort.

This event is crystal clear in my mind. Not only for the praise I received. But I also remember a very different reaction.

Our media manager, Kate Hutchinson, expressed her objection to what was happening.

Hutchinson, who departed this role not long after the tour and later worked for the AFL, faced criticism for leading the players into what turned out to be self-incriminating press conferences. Bancroft's account of her moral objections to what was happening is a significant rebuttal of suggestions that the tampering was simply an escalation of a broader culture of gamesmanship.

I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.

I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up.

Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it.

I cannot speak for Kate's thoughts beyond what I remember her saying and doing. She deserves the opportunity to give her own account.

But her reaction is important because it completely challenges the idea that nobody had an opportunity to question what was happening.

We did. I did. And I chose to continue.

South Africa ultimately won the Test, with AB de Villiers playing a magnificent innings that helped turn the match decisively in their favour.

Whatever advantage we thought we were gaining, it wasn't enough. We had compromised our integrity and still lost.

South Africa's AB de Villiers helped turn the match in South Africa's favour. ( )

FROM PORT ELIZABETH TO CAPE TOWN

There was a substantial break between the second and third Tests.

I remember spending time exploring South Africa. I went swimming with sharks, visited Camps Bay, walked alone to the top of Table Mountain and enjoyed a day visiting wineries around Stellenbosch with teammates.

They are memories that should have been among the highlights of my first Test tour of South Africa.

Or the fact that I probably played the best innings of my career in the first innings of that Cape Town Test match. I scored 76 off 103 balls against Philander, Rabada, Morkel and Maharaja.

Instead, I now look back on that period knowing what I had been doing on the field.

The sandpaper had become part of what I perceived to be my responsibility within the team. I was worried about it.

Before the Cape Town Test, I remember speaking with Kate Hutchinson at training.

I asked what would happen if I was caught tampering with the ball. She did not want to engage in that conversation because of the seriousness of the consequences, but her response was "not good" and walked off.

Cameron Bancroft of Australia talks to the umpire on the third day of the third cricket test between South Africa and Australia at Newlands Stadium. ( )

CAPE TOWN: THE MOMENT EVERYTHING UNRAVELLED

The changing rooms at Newlands was unusual its layout, something Usman has described in his book.

I remember sitting next to Usman and Tim Paine in the smaller change room.

It has been documented that a coach approached me during our fielding innings telling me that I needed to do more with the sandpaper on the ball to get it to swing. That coach was David Saker and it is true.

Once again the same conversations we had on the field in Port Elizabeth continued. Me asking for feedback from Starcy, Pat, Josh and Mitch about working on the ball like the Test earlier.

They all told me what I was doing wasn't enough.

The same feedback was given behind the stumps when I asked Tim and guys in the slips.

This Test match it wasn't as effective using sandpaper due to the conditions and moisture. The conditions were difficult for reverse swing. The central wicket square was green, and the ball wasn't behaving in the way we wanted.

I continued trying to alter it.

The conversations I remember having with the bowlers about the ball's movement have troubled me enormously in the years since.

When I later heard public statements denying knowledge of sandpaper being used, I struggled to reconcile those denials with my memories.

I recognise there is a distinction between knowing a ball is reversing, suspecting it has been altered and knowing specifically that sandpaper has been used.

This is a significant caveat, for the sake of the bowlers, in that it permits they may have taken the same approach as captain Steve Smith and not wanted to know the details of what was occurring.

Then came the moment the cameras caught me. The sandpaper was exposed. And everything changed.

Peter Handcombe ran out at the drinks break after I'd been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants.

He said to me: "I think it's time I take that off you now". And Pete was doing his job after Boof shouted to him on the walkie talkie "get the f***ing sandpaper off Bangers now".

In my opinion, if he didn't know he wouldn't have said that.

And if it wasn't clear enough before, then it was obvious now.

Once again. WE ALL KNEW.

Captain Steven Smith and Cameron Bancroft (L) speak at a press conference in South Africa. ( )

THE PRESS CONFERENCE AND ANOTHER LIE

After I was caught in Cape Town, there were frantic conversations about how we should respond.

I remember there being a preference among some people to wait until the following day, to sleep on what had happened and consider a more measured public response.

Steve Smith wanted to address the situation immediately. He believed owning up to the incident would help contain the damage and allow us to move forward.

Steve just wanted to clear it so he could focus on batting. I went with him because I believed I needed to accept responsibility for my actions.

But even then, we did not tell the complete truth.

Before the press conference, I recall David Saker specifically warning against identifying sandpaper as the material used.

Other coaches, management and players agreed, some disagreed. "We cannot say we used sandpaper".

In the wake of Khawaja's book being published, Lehmann said he couldn't recall discussions about collective responsibility. "I don't remember that," Lehmann said. "There were two change rooms obviously, and there were meetings going on everywhere. To be perfectly honest I was in meetings with Cricket Australia a lot. That could have been the case, I don't know. I'm not saying yes or no to that one. There will be different points of view everywhere on this whole matter."

We listened to that advice and we followed it. There was concern about the implications of that admission. So we acknowledged ball-tampering while giving an inaccurate account of the material involved, describing tape and material collected from the ground.

It was another lie. One told while we were supposedly taking responsibility.

I look back at that press conference with enormous regret. We were frightened. We were under pressure. We were trying to manage a situation that was rapidly getting away from us.

THE INVESTIGATION AND THE SILENCE

The remainder of the Cape Town Test was intense.

There were private conversations, uncertainty about what would happen next and an overwhelming sense that our world was falling apart. The Prime Minister even weighed in.

Indeed, Turnbull called the incident "a shocking affront to Australia" and his emphatic reaction was seen by many as a factor in setting Cricket Australia on the path to heavy-handed punishments for the players who accepted blame. "This cheating is a disgrace, we all know that, it is a terrible disgrace," Turnbull said at the time. "Cricket Australia is dealing with it, they have to investigate it and they have to continue to act decisively and emphatically. Where do we want to get to? I'll tell you where we want to get to, we want to get to the point where we can all say once again, not rhetorically but heartfelt and with sincerity, that cricket is a fair game, cricket is a game that is synonymous with a fair go and fair play, that's what has to happen." "They now have to make sure that this great national game, this great international game, that is synonymous with fair play, is once again a game that is played by champions that everybody can look up to."

After the match, I remember a lengthy meeting involving players and staff on the tour.

We discussed how to respond to the scandal and the information that would need to be acknowledged publicly. By then, it was clear that the use of sandpaper could no longer be concealed.

Nobody in that meeting stood up and said they had been completely unaware of my use of sandpaper. Not one person.

Contrary everyone started to give me advice about what I should say and what I shouldn't say to minimise the damage on the team related with the sandpaper saga.

This is in many ways the most damaging passage of Bancroft's account, albeit the precise chronology is hard to pair with Khawaja's account of a similar meeting. If it is a true account, it completely dismantles Cummins's claim that there was never any discussion of collective responsibility, and suggests instead that other players were content for Bancroft to take the blame.

I had convinced myself that I was carrying out a role for the benefit of the team. Now I was facing the possibility that my international career might be over.

As it turns out I ended up becoming the scapegoat for the entire team.

Bowlers Pat Cummins (right) and Mitchell Starc released a joint statement denying they knew sandpaper had been taken onto the field. ( )

TWO WORDS THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING

In 2021, while playing county cricket for Durham, I gave an interview to The Guardian. During that conversation, I was asked about the awareness of the Australian bowlers.

This interview, with veteran journalist Donald McRae, was headlined: Cameron Bancroft on the ball-tampering scandal: 'I lost control of my values'

I was caught off guard. I had spent years trying to move forward, trying to focus on my cricket and trying not to reopen the events of South Africa.

When pressed, I answered the question of awareness as "self-explanatory". I had not intended to make a major public revelation. But those few words reignited the entire controversy.

Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon subsequently released a joint statement denying that they knew sandpaper had been taken onto the field to alter the ball before the television footage appeared at Newlands.

The statement read: "We pride ourselves on our honesty. So it's been disappointing to see that our integrity has been questioned by some journalists and past players in recent days in regard to the Cape Town Test of 2018. "We have already answered questions many times on this issue, but we feel compelled to put the key facts on the record again: We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands

And to those who, despite the absence of evidence, insist that 'we must have known' about the use of a foreign substance simply because we are bowlers, we say this: The umpires during that Test match, Nigel Llong and Richard Illingworth, both very respected and experienced umpires, inspected the ball after the images surfaced on the TV coverage and did not change it because there was no sign of damage. "None of this excuses what happened on the field that day at Newlands. It was wrong and it should never have happened. "We've all learned valuable lessons and we'd like to think the public can see a change for the better in terms of the way we play, the way we behave and respect the game. Our commitment to improving as people and players will continue. "We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. "It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."

Reading that statement was deeply painful.

I had memories of conversations on the field in Port Elizabeth and Newlands, feedback about the ball and shared celebrations that made the statement difficult for me to digest.

Yet I also knew that I had never publicly given a full account of those conversations. I did this for the same reason Usman never spoke, Dave never spoke and for what has transpired in the last week Mitch Marsh in his interview before the ODI series against England never said anything.

That reason is the want and desire to represent Australia. To do so goes against the story of events, puts CA under pressure and the lies which were already told.

In June 2018, Cricket Australia CEO James Sutherland gave 12 months' notice of his resignation from the job. Team high performance manager Pat Howard also departed, as did coach Darren Lehmann.

That is the contradiction I have wrestled with for years.

I felt hurt by the public response, the reaction of those bowlers and finding meaning in my life post it.

THE CAREER I THOUGHT I COULD REBUILD

When I accepted my punishment in 2018, I believed that Dave, Steve and I taking sole responsibility for the entire team, serving my suspension and demonstrating that I had changed would eventually allow me to rebuild my international career.

I also hoped that the people who had shared that dressing room would understand the responsibility I had taken on.

I believed that, with time, my performances and conduct might earn me another opportunity to represent Australia.

There have been periods in Sheffield Shield cricket when I was out of touch and wasn't at the top of the list for Test selection.

But there were other times I genuinely believed I had done enough to warrant selection. I have continued to train, compete, make runs and pursue the dream of wearing the baggy green again. Yet the opportunities I hoped for have not materialised in the way I expected.

Selection is complicated. There are cricketing reasons, competing players, different conditions and decisions that I have not been part of. For many years I believed I would be selected because I trusted the selection process.

But I would be lying if I said I had never wondered whether the unresolved tension surrounding these events in South Africa had played a part.

Because in spite of having scored the most hundreds of any player in the competition in the last six years, including featuring in the top-three run scorers for over half that period I have never had a look in.

A pointed comment made by former Test opener Shane Watson in recent days was that in a selection sense, fellow opener Usman Khawaja benefited more than any other player from the suspension of openers Bancroft and David Warner, although this was a factor beyond Khawaja's control.

After my "self-explanatory" public statement in 2021, I felt increasingly uncomfortable around some of the people involved. I wondered whether my presence in an Australian dressing room might bring back questions that others wanted to leave behind. I wondered whether the easiest option was simply not to select me which I believe to be quite unfair in my opinion.

The hardest part has been feeling that nobody fully understood my perspective and the complete truth that was South Africa and the sandpapergate. This includes Australian selectors and coaching staff making these cricket decisions.

I made a terrible decision because I wanted to belong in the Australian team.

I made mistake, I owned my mistakes, I served the severe punishment, I came back, scored runs, in the hope I would be selected again in the Australian team. Which has not eventuated yet.

And in the years that followed, I have sometimes felt that this incident has left me permanently an outsider.

Former Cricket Australia chief executive James Sutherland gestures during a news conference at South African hotel in 2018 ( )

CONCLUSION

For eight years, I suffered silently. I cannot change the past. But I can change what I do now.

The release of Usman's book has reassured me that the events of South Africa have never truly been resolved.

There are still unanswered questions, conflicting recollections and people who have lived with the consequences in different ways.

I do not claim that my account alone settles every question.

This is the truth that I am now prepared to give openly and in full.

As the person at the centre of this, all I am doing this now is because I can't handle the burden anymore of carrying for everyone what happened in South Africa.

Nobody has pushed me to write this, I don't feel obliged, or to benefit financially by sharing this.

Michael Clarke in an interview last week said: "Now we've got this opportunity. I would just like to see whatever the truth is for it all to come out, allow people to finally tell the truth, and move on. Fans have not moved on".

And, as I wrote earlier, I am looking forward to being part of the CA forum and to speak as specific and detailed as possible without being general.

I am inspired by Michael Clarke's comment and I agree the fans deserve this.

This is my responsibility.

And here it is.
