title: Economists warn Australia is showing the hallmarks of recession
text:
As Christmas presents go, it's probably a dead heat with a lump of coal.

But mortgage holders may at least take some comfort that the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) seemingly relentless campaign to make them poorer is over for this year, and possibly the next.

Financial markets have removed all bets of another pre-Christmas rate rise when the reserve board concludes its final meeting of 2026 on December 8.

After a gloomy jobs report, markets are now tipping Christmas 2027 will see interest rates at least one rate cut lower, and maybe two.

Grim outlook for job hunters

A lot can change between now and then, of course.

Any joy at a rates reprieve comes at the expense of the growing proportion of Australia's 15.5 million-strong labour force who are finding themselves without a seat in the game of musical chairs that is our jobs market.

For the first time since COVID, more than 750,000 Australians who were available and actively looking for work in October were unable to find it.

And that's before the impact of the RBA's latest rate hike this month.

The bank's latest forecasts tipped the official jobless rate to rise to 5.1 per cent by next Christmas. Well, in one leap, October's 0.2 percentage point rise in the jobless rate to 4.9 per cent gets us halfway there already.

Recession alarm bells ringing

Economists are now sounding the alarm about an increasing chance the RBA's campaign to cool inflationary pressures could tip the Australian economy into recession.

"Recession is clearly a concern," HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham said.

Indeed, there is a chance we are already in one, according to Betashares chief economist David Bassanese: "Consecutive large employment declines might suggest the economy already has one foot in recession."

If it quacks like a recession…

There are many different definitions of a recession.

In Australia, we tend to speak of two consecutive three-month periods in which economic output contracts (you might hear people saying "two quarters of negative GDP growth" but that's just a fancy way of saying the same thing).

The unemployment rate has ticked up more than expected. (Reuters: Brian Snyder)

In the US, the National Bureau of Economic Research, which officially dates American recessions, defines them more loosely as "a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy and that lasts more than a few months".

Are there alternatives to interest rate hikes? Mortgage holders reeling from five interest rate hikes this year are questioning whether there are other ways of controlling inflation.

A shrinking economy, of course, means fewer job opportunities.

So some economists prefer to say a recession is when the jobless rate rises by one percentage point.

Against that yardstick, Australia's jobless rate has now climbed 0.8 percentage points since its Christmas 2025 level of 4.1 per cent.

Which just about passes the "duck test". Namely, if it looks like a recession, swims like a recession and quacks like a recession, then it probably is a recession.

Loading

RBA to take stock

RBA governor Michele Bullock is adamant it is not the bank's intention to deliberately drive the economy into recession.

But even if we avoid the technical definition of recession, Bullock has already conceded interest rate hikes will make this a tough Christmas for many.

"It is going to make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer. Their spending can't grow very quickly, because their incomes aren't growing very quickly," she said.

The RBA is now expected to use its Christmas break to take stock of the impact of its five rate hikes this year.

But amid continued global disruptions, elevated oil prices and a falling Aussie dollar — which adds to domestic inflation — the path ahead for interest rates in 2027 is anyone's bet.

title: Live: PM's message to Putin as Russian leader meets with Xi and Trump
authors: Political Reporter Clare Armstrong In Beijing
North Asia Correspondent Natalie Whiting In Tokyo
China Correspondent Allyson Horn In Shenzhen
text:
When Donald Trump and Xi Jinping sit down for their meeting in Shenzhen, there's one subject neither will want to talk about: the alleged Chinese spying operation against recently resigned Nvidia chief Jensen Huang.

Ironically, AI is probably the issue the two most need to talk about.

The US and China will largely define how rapidly AI develops and develops in a way that minimises potential damage from "rogue agents".

They may talk about AI generally, but the real test of their preparedness to discuss the issue was shown when Xi visited Washington, and the two avoided coming up with any clear guidelines for AI.

Jensen Huang and Donald Trump have had a close relationship for some time. (Reuters: Evan Vucci, file photo)

The reality is both men, and both countries, are too competitive to want to give up any option that may be curbed by the other.

It's generally believed the US is leading the AI "race" — thanks largely to super chip giant Nvidia — and that China is six months behind.

Which is where the so-called spy scandal comes in. Reportedly, US intelligence believes Alice Huang (no relation) was working for China when she developed a relationship with Huang.

The US version is that Ms Huang used a company in Singapore — Megaspeed — to buy Nvidia chips using her "special relationship" with Mr Huang.

Trump says he's not even sure that Ms Huang was a spy. He's said that often attractive Chinese women are stereotyped as spies.

It is difficult to predict what Trump may do, but based on past meetings with Xi and other world leaders, he's shown a pattern of avoiding conflict.

Xi Jinping was hosted by Donald Trump at the White House earlier this year. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

The stories are legion of how he's confronted world leaders on the phone. His phone conversation with former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull was a major story.

But generally — with an exception for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy — Trump prefers not to confront world leaders in public.

He particularly wants a warm relationship with Xi.

It may change, but for the moment the general view in Washington is that Trump wants a meeting with the Chinese leader, accompanied by a warm photo-opportunity, rather than conflict on any issue, particularly allegations about an alleged Chinese spy.

title: Cheap Chinese EVs are causing havoc on the Australian used car market
text:
More used cars are for sale; they are selling for less, and petrol cars are losing value fastest.

These are insights from the latest industry data showing the impact of low-cost Chinese EVs on a second-hand car market dominated by petrol and diesel vehicle sales.

Dealerships are struggling to shift stock and say conditions are the "worst ever".

Some in the industry believe the value of used fossil fuel vehicles will continue to decline as EVs get cheaper and buyers look to save on fuel.

So, what does this mean for the value of your car?

And what vehicle types are likely to see the sharpest declines?

The year that reshaped the car market

Although new-car sales get the most attention, most Australians buy their cars on the second-hand market.

In 2026, changes in the new-car market rippled through auction houses, dealerships and online marketplaces that shift over 2 million used cars every year.

The war in Iran and high fuel prices, along with an influx of low-cost, heavily discounted Chinese brands, drove a surge in new EV sales.

Many of today's top-selling brands were unheard of a few years ago.

As EV uptake increased, used petrol and diesel vehicles flooded the second-hand market.

Low-cost new cars also put pressure on used car prices.

New Chinese SUVs were advertised for the typical asking price of a three-year-old Toyota Rav4, Steven Bragg, a motor industry adviser at Pitcher Partners, told the ABC.

"The Chinese SUV probably has better tech, better specs, and a new car warranty of eight years," he said.

He said dealerships found themselves stuck with stock that was rapidly losing value.

"It's the hardest conditions they've been through," Mr Bragg said.

"Even the GFC was better than this."

The Australian Automotive Dealers Association (AADA) wants to stop new brands entering the market.

"It's becoming more difficult to value some vehicles on the used car market because such is the rate of change," AADA chief executive James Voortman said.

Australians prefer to buy their cars second-hand, making the used-car market about twice the size of the new-car one. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Used cars always depreciate, but now some models are losing value faster than before.

Petrol cars (excluding hybrids and plug-in hybrids) lost five times more value in 2026 than in the previous year, according to data from the analytics platform AutoGrab.

Diesels lost about twice as much value in 2026 as hybrids and battery-electric vehicles, with SUVs faring worse than utes and four-wheel drives designed for heavy towing, data from online used car dealership Carma shows.

Some say this is the market correcting itself after used cars became overpriced during the pandemic.

But others argue these falls are a sign of big changes to come.

Will the value of used petrol and diesel cars keep falling this fast?

This is the big question, and there are many conflicting opinions.

Variables affecting depreciation rates include fuel prices and electric alternatives, inflation, and broader cost-of-living pressures.

"Most of the key industry data sources say it's likely used car prices will continue to fall for the foreseeable future," Mike Costello, an industry analyst at Cox Automotive, told the ABC.

He said demand for used diesel utes and large four-wheel drives should remain robust while there are few EV equivalents.

But other vehicle types "will probably fare differently".

" Selling a diesel mid-sized SUV in 2029 is going to be a potential challenge … These are uncharted waters that we are swimming towards. "

The EV industry's peak body, the EV Council, made a similar prediction.

"Demand for certain vehicle segments is going to evaporate and may evaporate quicker than people expect," EVC head of policy Aman Gaur said.

"I would just urge people who are buying petrol cars to be cautious about what the future demand might be, given the demand for petrol cars is decreasing, and the demand for electric cars is increasing."

Market segments already well served by EVs include hatchbacks, sedans and mid-size SUVs. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Sales of new petrol cars (excluding hybrids) have almost halved over six years.

But Fleet News director Marc Sibbald dismissed the idea Australians would flock to EVs.

"In five years time we'll still be struggling with charging infrastructure," Mr Sibbald said.

"There'll still be non-believers. There's my neighbour who thinks BYD is spying on them, the guys I drink with at the pub who think EVs are going to catch on fire."

EVs hit mainstream Electric cars have become mainstream in the past decade, making up one in four new car sales.

He advises fleet managers that petrol and diesel cars will depreciate at the long-term average rate.

Brendon Green, a general manager at Pickles Auctions, said fossil fuel vehicle resale values would not collapse.

"We anticipate a gradual shift in resale values rather than a dramatic decline, with the extent of any price movements varying across vehicle segments."

What about used EVs?

Used EVs tend to depreciate much faster than used fossil fuel cars, losing about half their value over three years.

The spike in EV demand in March meant they temporarily gained value, but industry data shows they are now losing value again.

But depreciation rates are hard to predict.

Cox Automotive's Mr Costello expected EVs would hold their value better as fears about severe battery degradation proved unfounded.

"We're seeing cars with 90–95 per cent of battery health remaining entering the second-hand market," he said.

Will new EVs keep getting cheaper?

The influx of low-cost Chinese brands in 2026 was the result of a combination of events that may not be repeated, Carma chief executive Lachlan MacGregor said.

Chinese domestic sales slumped, causing manufacturers to expand overseas just as the United States, Europe and Canada banned or limited vehicle imports.

"We've had the fierce forces of competition like no other market has had," he said.

Manufacturers cannot sell the cars any cheaper.

" I wouldn't say that I would forecast that EVs become cheaper again. In fact, with incentives rolling off, maybe they go up in price. "

The price of EVs in five years will depend largely on battery prices, which in turn depend on research outcomes and manufacturing advances that are hard to predict.

Another variable is what models manufacturers make available in Australia.

Small EVs with limited range are being sold in China for less than $10,000.

Mr Bragg said a car like this in the Australian market could collapse the value of used hatchbacks, but only if buyers thought it was as good as petrol models.

"If it's a Corolla-level-good vehicle for a great price, then 100 per cent it would impact the market."

While the future was uncertain, he said one thing was clear.

"It's never been a better time to buy a car."

title: Humble Ash Barty inducted into hall of fame
text:
Ash Barty has never been one to trumpet her achievements, so perhaps it was no surprise her election to the International Tennis Hall of Fame (ITHF) left the Australian delighted but wondering whether she truly belonged among the game's greats.

The three-time grand slam singles champion and former world number one will be formally inducted at a ceremony in Newport, Rhode Island, next August and take her place among luminaries including Roger Federer, Billie ‌Jean King and Margaret Court.

Nearly five years on from retirement but still only 30, Barty was touched to have personal messages of congratulations from nearly 20 Hall of Famers, including Federer and Martina Navratilova, as ITHF co-presidents Kim Clijsters and Patrick McEnroe gave her the news in a surprise call.

"I feel very, very ‌humbled and grateful. And to be honest, I've got a little bit of impostor syndrome, where I feel I don't quite belong," she told Reuters in a call from her home base in Queensland.

"The Hall of Fame is ‌for the absolute legends of our game, and I'm not sure I'm quite there."

Ash Barty won Wimbledon in 2021, the third Australian woman to do so after Margaret Court and Evonne Goolagong Cawley. (Getty: Clive Brunskill)

Few of her compatriots ‌would share that assessment of Barty, whose triumph at the 2022 Australian Open ended a 44-year wait for a homegrown women's singles champion.

The all-court player won grand slams on three different surfaces, claiming the 2019 French Open title and 2021 Wimbledon crown, and spent 114 consecutive weeks with the number one ranking.

Barty is the 35th Australian player, male or female, to be inducted into the Hall of Fame.

She will be inducted along with Japan's four-time Paralympic gold medallist and 50-time major ‌champion Shingo Kunieda, who was elected in the wheelchair tennis category.

Barty said her honour belonged as much to the team that accompanied her on her roller-coaster tennis journey, which included struggles with depression, a nearly two-year break from the game and a fascinating diversion as a professional cricketer.

"I'm probably most excited to tell my team because it ‌feels like it's as much for me ‌as it is for them," said Barty, now a mother to two small children.

Her retirement from tennis at 25, barely two months on from her Melbourne ‌Park triumph, has long fuelled speculation of whether she might one day come back.

Ash Barty (right) and Evonne Goolagong Cawley (left) are two of the eight Australian women to be inducted into the ITHF. (Getty Images: James D. Morgan)

The Hall of Fame includes players who balanced motherhood with grand slam glory in Court, Clijsters and Barty's mentor, Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

But a happy Barty said she had ‌no intention of joining them, being content and focused on family.

Asked whether her position had hardened from "never say never" to simply "never", she replied: "No, mate, it was always never."

And there were no regrets about retiring young.

"No, no, no, not one."

Barty had little to say about Serena Williams's return to tennis at the age of 44 and the American's motivation of having her kids see her play.

"My kids don't even know that I played tennis, and I'm sure that at the induction next year they'll wonder what's going on," she said.

"I'm deep in the trenches with my two little ones at the moment, and I ‌absolutely love it."

Barty will join ‌Goolagong Cawley as the second Indigenous Australian in the Hall of Fame, and hopes more will follow.

"I think if you can provide the opportunity and the platform for them to learn and grow, then hopefully, maybe one day, there's another young boy or girl being inducted into the Hall of Fame," she said.

Deputy legislative council president Steve Martin has taken the extraordinary step of clearing the public gallery following outbursts from WA Greens supporters during a debate over proposed legislation to ban forest mining. WA Greens MLC Jess Beckerling on Thursday proposed an amendment to the Mining Act 1978 and called for a ban to native forest mining. The Australian sharemarket’s losing streak continued on Thursday, with the local bourse falling for a sixth straight session and wiping out the rest of this year’s gains as global AI anxiety weighed on the mining and tech sectors and Australia reported its highest unemployment rate since 2021. The S&P/ASX 200 closed 91.40 points, or 1 per cent, lower at 8730.40, basically flat from its level at the start of the year. Mining heavyweights led the losses after the price of copper, seen as integral to the AI boom, plunged by almost 6 per cent overnight. The Australian dollar slid 0.5 per cent to $US66.86¢, also wiping out its gains for the year, on the back of the weak employment data. Global markets are on an unsteady footing as doubts over AI companies hover. AP The newly created AFR Real Economy index – which tracks 500 companies that mirror the ABS’ composition of the actual economy– was down 0.5 per cent, while the AFR Global 50, which tracks Australia’s top 50 companies with majority revenue from offshore, slumped 1.4 per cent. The Australian Bureau of Statistics’ labour force data showed the Reserve Bank’s aggressive tightening of monetary policy has hit the jobs market, with the unemployment rate spiking to 4.9 per cent last month. Unemployment rose by 0.2 percentage points, reaching its highest level since 2021.

Advertisement

The weaker-than-expected labour market reinforced bets that the RBA has ended its interest-rate hike cycle and will pivot to cuts next year, sending the Aussie dollar to its lowest since early January. Related Article Analysis

Interest rates One foot in recession: The unemployment numbers that blow up the RBA’s case for hikes “This release all but closes the door on a December hike and shifts the debate to how long rates stay at their peak,” said Sunny Nguyen, head of the Australian economics team at Moody’s Analytics. While prospects of an interest rate reprieve usually boost sentiment, it wasn’t enough to dispel dark clouds over the AI trade, which has been driving global markets this year and is faltering amid fears the heavily indebted and interdependent sector could also make them crash. Despite those concerns, AI frontier lab Anthropic – the company behind chatbot Claude – released the pricing for its Wall Street float. Bloomberg said the stock will be set at $US83 per share, above its target range of $US70 to $US78, valuing the company at $US1.5 trillion ($2.2 trillion). The company is set to start trading on Friday morning (AEDT).

Mining stocks plunged yet again on the ASX, with BHP down another 3.7 per cent and Rio Tinto down 4.1 per cent. Copper steadied after plunging almost 6 per cent overnight – the biggest drop since April 2025 – on a sharp unwinding of bullish bets tied to AI and US tariffs. The red metal has lost 12 per cent so far in November, fuelled by growing doubts over the durability of AI-related spending and fading expectations for US tariffs on refined copper. Related Article Opinion

AI Could AI become the new subprime crisis? Anthropic investors are undeterred Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Gold miners also extended losses, with Northern Star slumping 5.7 per cent, Evolution Mining plunging 7.3 per cent and Newmont down 4.6 per cent. Gold wavered near a 14-month low after Federal Reserve officials signalled its interest-rate hikes are likely to stretch into next year, making the non-yielding metal less attractive for investors. Financial stocks were holding up better, with Commonwealth Bank up 0.4 per cent, while Westpac dropped 0.2 per cent, ANZ Bank slipped 0.1 per cent and National Australia Bank dropped 0.9 per cent. Energy stocks finished lower, with Woodside Energy down 2 per cent, Santos down 1.9 per cent and refiner Ampol down 2.7 per cent. Oil had slumped overnight, but steadied as traders assessed the outlook for the US-Iran conflict, including the possibility of fresh attacks against Tehran, with Brent holding above $US92 a barrel. US President Donald Trump is weighing plans for further strikes, the New York Times reported, citing US and Israeli officials. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing him to join a four- to seven-day campaign, it said.

Technology stocks were mixed, with local AI-related stocks NextDC and Megaport up 4.3 per cent and 3.5 per cent following Anthropic’s higher-than-expected IPO price. Software maker WiseTech dropped 0.9 per cent and Xero was flat. In New York trading, the S&P 500 dragged Wall Street to its longest losing streak since June, with AI stocks continuing to weigh on global indexes. The S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent after zigzagging between gains and losses through the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite added 0.4 per cent. Related Article Insolvency General Pants collapses after years of trouble Nvidia was once again at the centre of Wall Street’s moves. Its stock initially jumped 2.7 per cent after the chip company reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, but that gain was wiped out and it closed 2.9 per cent lower. Perhaps more importantly, it also gave a forecast for revenue in the current quarter that was better than expected. The question is whether Nvidia’s big growth can continue despite the turmoil created by the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. He had an immense personality that drew attention and investment to AI, and he built Nvidia into a company so big that it helped to fund some of the industry’s growth itself.

“Our momentum is real,” Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, told investors and financial analysts after announcing the company’s latest results. “Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us. And employees are committed. We’ve got this.” The encouraging numbers and words coming from Nvidia failed to create lasting gains for the price of its stock or for others across the industry. title: I expected juicy gossip. I didn’t expect one of the year’s best memoirs

CultureBooksReview I expected juicy gossip. I didn’t expect one of the year’s best memoirs Robert Moran November 19, 2026 — 5:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

“Whoever tells the story first controls the narrative,” writes Sofia Franklyn in Daddy Issues, her memoir detailing her own side of her spectacular exit from the hit podcast Call Her Daddy. For Franklyn, it’s a hard-won insight. It’s widely known as the “biggest podcast fumble in history” – Franklyn ostensibly bungling herself out of a deal that her one-time partner, Alex Cooper, has spun into a $US500 million media and lifestyle empire, the Unwell Network. Franklyn has been on the losing end of the public narrative ever since. Sofia Franklyn’s memoir Daddy Issues is best described as revenge served ice-cold. The fallout was initially framed by Cooper, who in 2020 posted a slick video telling the podcast’s #DaddyGang fans that Franklyn’s greed, laziness and subservience to a man (her boyfriend at the time, HBO executive Peter Nelson, the book’s tragic collateral damage) were to blame for their split. It was then cemented by the pair’s original boss, Barstool Sports kingpin Dave Portnoy, who framed Franklyn as a messy, entitled brat in his tacky memoir (please, let us never speak of it again), Cancel Me If You Can. Franklyn’s late entry – revenge served ice-cold – spins another perspective to the saga, detailing Cooper’s behind-the-scenes backstabbing and calculated manoeuvring. She frames Cooper as a Gatsby-meets-Brutus character: secretive, unreliable, a ruthless social climber who’d mysteriously cut ties with her past.

Advertisement

Of course, it was all good at first. Early scenes highlight their sisterly (almost sapphic, Franklyn implies) camaraderie as Manhattan transplants. Later chapters drop in digs that explain the book’s opening revelation that Cooper’s husband, Matt Kaplan, called Franklyn’s publisher saying Cooper was threatening to sue before the book was even written. “It’s the first I’ve heard from Alex in six years. The first since the fallout, when she stopped responding to my text messages,” writes Franklyn. The icky, enticing dirty laundry is worth the price of admission. And Franklyn is such a thoughtful and emotive writer, naturally comfortable with contradictions, that even those not so invested in this Rashomon for the world of obnoxious Millennial podcasting will be adding Daddy Issues to the great canon of messy memoirs, alongside Elizabeth Wurtzel’s Prozac Nation, Cat Marnell’s How to Murder Your Life and Julia Fox’s Down the Drain. Look, I’m surprised, too. Starting from her wild childhood (drinking, drugs, sex, jail time), Franklyn deftly underscores why the betrayal hit so hard. Sure, $200 million is probably most of it, but it also comes down to the ravaging of a belief she held sacred: that in a world of horrible men, women always had her back. Call Her Daddy’s Alex Cooper and husband Matt Kaplan. Getty Images for Netflix Growing up, the male presence in Franklyn’s life was either negligible or volatile. Her mother, an Argentinian immigrant who worked at a DV shelter, had her young. Her biological father, a Spanish man named Joaquin, was entirely absent. Her stepfather, Tom, a New Zealander, struggled with drug abuse. Elsewhere, her experiences with men have been violent or criminal.

Advertisement

The stalwarts in her life, unconditionally supportive, have been women: her mum, her grandma, her mum’s sisters and Spanish friends, her childhood friend Mia. It’s why, when the Call Her Daddy shit hits the fan, it’s unfathomable to Franklyn that another woman would do this to her. Photo: As she herself writes, Franklyn’s smarts have been underestimated due to her now trademark vocal fry (listen to the audiobook, it’s worth it). Her sharp imagery puts you in the centre of her paranoid spiral, to the point where she’s accusing her own mum of spying on her. A scene where she’s begging Cooper to let her back on the show, realising she has no alternative path, is gruesome. Another, where she’s reacting in real-time to Cooper’s viral “The Truth About Call Her Daddy” video, is devastating. “Lost a friend? I’m right here. Just answer my texts. I’m waving the white flag,” she writes. By the book’s end, after her desperation is exhausted – like all good writers, Franklyn has no censor when it comes to depicting herself at her most pitiful and depraved – that white flag takes on new symbolism: a clean slate. When Franklyn – broken and literally unwell in a pharmacy where she’s shopping for medicine – comes across Cooper’s signature on a hydration drink, she laughs at the cosmic absurdity.

Advertisement

Much of the book, like that scene, plays like a parting shot at whatever remains of Call Her Daddy’s #girlboss-era feminism (an easier stance to take when you didn’t land the bag). It’s also bait from someone so unscrupulously written out of the main story: Alex Cooper will surely have to re-engage at some point, which you imagine is all Sofia Franklyn ever wanted. It’s the saga we need and deserve. Daddy Issues by Sofia Franklyn is published by Simon and Schuster ($37). The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

title: ‘She believed it was wrong’: The team staffer who spoke up against sandpaper
text:

SportCricketBall tampering ‘She believed it was wrong’: The team staffer who spoke up against sandpaper Chris Barrett Updated November 19, 2026 — 5:03pm ,first published 2:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In the week before the third Test at Newlands in 2018, Australian team media manager Kate Hutchison dropped her own bombshell. Over lunch in Stellenbosch, a famed wine region just east of Cape Town, she told reporters covering the series that she was resigning after six years with Cricket Australia. Loading She was leaving not as a result of the Australian team’s use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball, which we now know had been going on since the previous match in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha. Instead, she had tired of their out-of-control behaviour, which had spiralled in South Africa, and of the demands of being on the road for more than half the year.

Advertisement

Eight years later, Hutchison has been cast by Cameron Bancroft as the lone voice of dissent against Australia’s ploy to cheat on the tour by using sandpaper to rough up one side of the ball. In a blow-by-blow account of the scandal that has propelled CA and the Test captaincy of Pat Cummins into crisis, the former opener describes Hutchison “expressing her objection to what was happening” in a team huddle on the morning of day three in Gqeberha. Kate Hutchison with then-captain Steve Smith at Adelaide Oval in 2017. Ryan Pierse His use of sandpaper late on day two was being discussed in the group at the time, Bancroft said. “I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion,” he said of Hutchison.

Advertisement

“I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up. Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it.” Bancroft also referred to a conversation with Hutchison at training before the next Test in Cape Town, where he was caught with sandpaper on the field. Loading “I asked what would happen if I was caught tampering with the ball. She did not want to engage in that conversation because of the seriousness of the consequences, but her response was, ‘Not good’, and she walked off,” he said. Hutchison, who went on to work for Swimming Australia and the AFL and is now head of corporate communications for the RACV, declined to comment on Thursday.

Advertisement

Sources who spoke on the condition of anonymity said she has no dispute with Bancroft’s account but is uncomfortable being presented as a moral compass of some kind after the fact. Like most media managers, she has no desire to be the story herself. A straight shooter, it comes as little surprise to those who know Hutchison that she would have spoken up about what she thought. Kate Hutchison (right) with swimmer Ariarne Titmus at the Australian Open last year. Getty Images As a media professional, her role didn’t involve being present when the team was devising or discussing tactics. But she would have been acutely aware that such brazen manipulation of the ball could backfire publicly if it was exposed, although even she could not have anticipated the extent of the fallout and for how long it would endure.

Advertisement

Hutchison, like many in the 30-plus touring party in South Africa of players, coaches and staff, has wrestled with the events of 2018 while abiding by an effective omertà in the years since, according to the same sources. A New Zealander who joined CA in 2012 and handled media duties for an Australian under-19s tour and a women’s World Cup before joining the men’s team set-up, she had come under intense scrutiny at the time over the notorious press conference at Newlands in which Bancroft and Steve Smith lied. Darren Lehmann (right) and bowling coach David Saker have been drawn into the scandal by Cameron Bancroft. AP Their dishonesty dug them into a deeper hole and was such a disaster that one leading television newsman said the media manager should be sacked. However, it had long been suggested that Smith had been advised not to go to the press conference that day while in such an emotional state, and Usman Khawaja confirmed in his autobiography that he and Hutchison had tried to talk the captain out of it.

Advertisement

Related Article Ball tampering Lehmann dodges question on Bancroft claims, leaves commentary box When it became clear that there was no changing Smith’s mind, it’s understood she was among those who urged him and Bancroft not to lie. This masthead revealed last week that bowling coach David Saker had allegedly told them “You can’t say sandpaper”, and Bancroft recalls Saker “specifically warning against identifying sandpaper as the material used”. The fact that they followed that advice – and overlooked the counsel of others – is evidence of the culture of denial and the toxic bubble that existed around the team under the control of head coach Darren Lehmann. Bancroft said he “cannot speak for Kate’s thoughts beyond what I remember her saying and doing” and that “she deserves the opportunity to give her own account”. Having well and truly moved on from her stint with cricket, Hutchison has no intention of doing that.

title: The best Brisbane sandwiches of the past 12 months
text:
Advertisement

Eating outSandwich Watch The best Brisbane sandwiches of the past 12 months From a Hainanese chicken sandwich and a fancy chip butty, to one made with pizza dough, these are the past year’s essential sangers. Matt Shea November 19, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

We joked last year that we should rename Sandwich Watch to Sandwich Search, such is the number of dragons you sometimes need to slay to get to the royalty around town. But we also said a rising tide lifts all boats, and that really rung true when reflecting on what we ate between two slices of bread in the past 12 months. The quality has definitely stepped up around Brisbane, as the bogus recommendations stepped off. Uncle Don makes a contender for the city’s best katsu sando. Markus Ravik October ticked off this column’s second anniversary. To mark the milestone, here are the best sandwiches we’ve eaten in the past 12 months. Jane’s Deli’s Hainanese chicken sandwich

Advertisement

Why hasn’t someone thought of this before? Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Jane’s Deli Hainanese chicken sandwich is one of the best in town. Markus Ravik Hainanese chicken is, of course, usually associated with chicken rice, a national dish in Singapore (alongside chilli crab) that’s also enormously popular in neighbouring Malaysia. One caveat about sticking it in a sandwich, though, is that much of the flavour of chicken rice often comes from the rice and typical condiments such as spicy garlic chilli, dark soy and ginger sauce. But Jane’s owners and chefs Jianne Jeong and Leaham Claydon have this covered. Related Article Brisbane’s best sanger? This Hainanese chicken number is a contender

Advertisement

Let’s start with that bread. It’s a pain de mie, the silky, fluffy French-style sandwich loaf characterised by its soft interior and thin crust, which will reaffirm your faith in the humble white-bread sanger. The pain de mie is given a liberal smear of mayonnaise, a layer of salted cucumber, and shredded iceberg. For the protein, whole chickens are hot brined with shaoxing, ginger and spring onions. The resulting bird is juicy but firm, and the skin has been left on, again recalling a traditional chicken rice. The final flourish is a drizzle of Mama Liu’s chilli oil (which is on the shelves at Jane’s Deli) for a big dash of umami. Related Article Brisbane’s best sandwiches? Here are our top picks of the past year We bang on in this column sometimes about chef-made sandwiches, but this is absolutely that, with a clear, purposeful flavour profile. Please go eat it. Olli Italiano’s mortadella panuozzo

Advertisement

Like so many great sandwiches, the beauty of Olli Italiano’s mortadella panuozzo’s (a “pizza sandwich”) lies in its simplicity. The mortadella, supplied by Selecta Food Group, is made by an Italian family in Melbourne. This is complemented with a fistful of springy rocket, gooey stracciatella from Byron Bay Mozzarella, and a liberal sprinkle of pistachio – as much for texture as it is flavour. Olli Italiano’s Panuozzo are huge, and therefore excellent value. Morgan Roberts Simple, except it’s wrapped inside an almighty pizza base made with Italian 00 flour, filled with fior di latte and cooked fast at 350 degrees in this East Brisbane restaurant’s drop-door pizza oven to produce a bubbly, crispy Neapolitan-ish crust. It’s then finished with a generous sprinkle of pecorino for a bit of seasoning. And that’s it. Related Article You need to eat this mortadella pizza sanger that’s as big as your face

Advertisement

It makes for a luscious, deeply satisfying sandwich that’s as big as your face, yet easy to eat with one hand (after the chefs cut it in two, at least). Anytime Coffee’s deli sandwich Anytime Coffee’s sandwiches have always been at least pretty good, but it was its brilliant deli sandwich that registered with this column recently. Anytime’s deli sandwich. Markus Ravik Deli sandwiches require precision and Anytime’s take is about as precise as it gets – which is impressive when you discover how much is going on under the hood. For meats, Anytime uses leg ham, salami cotto and capocollo sourced from Rayner’s Meats in New Farm. That’s layered with crunchy rocket, pickled red onion, and a green olive and guindilla mix that’s arguably the sandwich’s secret weapon.

Advertisement

Sealing it all off is some provolone dolce. It’s there for its creamy texture and to protect the bread, which is why the Anytime crew has opted for a milder take on the semi-hard Italian cheese. Related Article Finally, the deli sandwich we’ve been searching for in Brisbane Talking bread, all this is squeezed between two slices of a light-rye sourdough tin loaf that’s produced by NYC Bagel for Anytime from a Riser Bread recipe. If not the perfect deli sandwich, it’s pretty damn close. Nali Kitchen’s braised beef brisket sandwich

Advertisement

Imagine the messy hot roast beef sandwich from the corner carvery of your youth, but given the best kind of glow-up. Nali Kitchen's braised brisket sandwich recalls the corner carvery beef sanger of your youth. Markus Ravik That’s the approach at Nali Kitchen in Gresham Lane in the CBD. Here, the brisket is braised rather than smoked (“we are not a smokehouse and don’t try to be”, owner and chef Matthew Van Der Zwan says), left overnight in a stock that’s kept “pretty muted” to help let the quality of the protein shine through. Van Der Zwan prefers Riverina Angus rump cap. Cleverly, the accompaniments across all of Nali Kitchen’s sandwiches are the same – charred onion, rocket, salsa verde and aioli – keeping the focus squarely on the quality of the meat. Everything is then slapped between two slices of focaccia that are soft enough to soak up any decadence that might try to slip out. Related Article Introducing the roast beef sanger of your dreams

Advertisement

Brisket is a relatively heavy cut of beef, partly because of the connective collagen that holds the muscles together, and partly because of its inherently high fat content. But the 16-hour braise leaves it juicy and tender, and the rocket and salsa verde give it a lovely herbaceous lift. The whole thing is then tied together by the sweet, nutty aioli, and it eats like a dream. Sunny Side Sandwiches’ eggplant offering Sunny Side Sandwiches has evolved over the years. The menu has expanded, then been reduced. Certain menu items have come, then gone again. Sunny Side Sandwiches’ eggplant offering. Morgan Roberts But according to co-owner Mack Bowers, there’s one that hasn’t changed – the eggplant sandwich.

Advertisement

It’s a variation on the triple-store setup’s star chicken schnitty sandwich, using the same chopped iceberg lettuce dressed in Japanese mayo, dill, parsley and chives; the same bread and butter pickles; the same shokupan bread; and then a “magic sprinkle” of the same signature seasoning, which features salt, nutritional yeast, Korean chilli flakes, and “a few other little secret herbs and spices”. In the middle, though, instead of chook there are two slices of eggplant that have been bathed in saltwater, panko crumbed, then stored in the freezer to help them set before being tossed in the frier. Related Article Brisbane’s best vegetarian sanger? This glorious thing is a contender The result is a contender for Brisbane’s best vegetarian sandwich. There’s the crispness of the eggplant, the crunch of the iceberg, the acid of the pickles, the velvety texture of the mayo with its tangy stack of herbs. And then there’s the deep, deep umami of the “magic sprinkle”. Still, for us, the shokupan is the real star here. It’s baked in-house, meaning it’s ultra-consistent and able to be sliced thinly while maintaining its integrity.

Advertisement

Naldham Terrace’s French beef baguette with dipping sauce There are a lot of great sandwiches around town at the moment, but not so many great French dips, where roast beef is stuffed into a crusty French baguette and served with a broth on the side. Until now, that is. Naldham Terrace’s French beef baguette with dipping sauce (beer optional). Markus Ravik Introducing, the Naldham Terrace French beef baguette with dipping sauce. Served outside on the ground floor at the greenery-lined Naldham House, it’s one of the best sandwiches you can get in the CBD. There’s almost nothing to this sanger: a baguette, some steak, caramelised onions and seeded mustard. But also, that’s selling it short.

Advertisement

The baguette is a tight little number baked daily by Eustralis, a specialist European food supplier, that’s been crisped just so for serving. The steak is a generous stack of S. Kidman two-to-three score flank, cooked medium rare and basted in the pan in butter, garlic and thyme. And the seeded mustard is Covinor, a quality French brand. Related Article This classy French steak sanga comes with a luscious dipping broth The Naldham chefs have nailed pulling it all together. There’s the crisp crunch of the baguette, the maillard, and the juiciness of the grilled flank, the sweetness from the caramelised onion, and the tangy vinegar of the mustard. Then there’s the side of broth, which is a heavenly bowl of stocky goodness. It has the right consistency to coat the sandwich without overpowering what’s slapped inside. And it’s dead simple to eat. Baguette sangers can get unwieldy but this is easy to manage, and the flank is tender enough that you won’t return to the office looking like you’ve been in a food fight.

Advertisement

Lindy’s Po Boys’ shrimp po’ boy Originating in New Orleans in 1929 as a cheap (or free) meal for striking streetcar workers, a po’ boy is similar to a submarine sandwich but defined by a more French-leaning roll that’s similar to a traditional baguette but lighter and fluffier inside. Lindy’s Po Boys’ shrimp po’ boy. Markus Ravik Typical fillings are prawns (shrimp, of course, in US parlance), roast beef and Louisiana hot sausage, and a traditional sandwich might be “dressed” with lettuce, tomato, pickles and mayonnaise. Steve Lind fell in love with po’ boys when travelling as a musician in 2016 and Lindy’s Po Boys was eventually born earlier this year. This column caught it on its third pop-up at Camp Hill Bowls Club.

Advertisement

On the menu was a pork sausage po’ boy and a shrimp po’ boy. It’s the latter we think you need to eat ASAP. The bread is made to Lind’s specs by Norman Park’s Golden K Bakery. It’s crisp on the outside (without being banh mi crunchy) and soft and pillowy on the inside – tasty, textural, moreish. Related Article This shrimp po’ boy is the perfect Brisbane sandwich. Here’s why For the dressing, Lind uses a moderate amount of iceberg lettuce, a few slices of tomato, and Fehlbergs burger pickles. He then gives each bun a squirt of Hellmann’s mayonnaise, Heinz tomato sauce, and Louisiana Hot Sauce for “acidity and sweetness”. For prawns, there’s nothing fancy, with Lind opting for wild-caught prawns from the supermarket so he can pile plenty of them into the sandwich. The batter, though, is special – a combination of plain flour, corn starch, and then cornflour for a dash of extra colour.

Advertisement

The result has all that texture from the fried prawns (which remain juicy inside), crispy iceberg and precision baked bread, but then stacks of acid, and salt and sweetness from the dressings and sauces. Also, unlike a banh mi or other baguette-based sandwiches, it’s a cinch to eat. We’ll keep you posted about the next pop-up. Sincerity by Jacorey’s chilli tuna mayo sandwich What initially attracted us to this brilliant sandwich was – counterintuitively, perhaps – its relative practicality when compared to its more Instagrammable stablemates at Upper Mt Gravatt’s Sincerity by Jacorey (the ebi katsu, in particular, is a real peacock of a sanger). Sincerity by Jacorey’s chilli tuna mayo sandwich. Markus Ravik

Advertisement

It might sound like a spicy tuna toastie but it’s much more than that. Co-owner Jamie Kim mixes skipjack tuna with kewpie mayo and a bunch of spices to create the silky chilli tuna mix at the heart of the sandwich (Skipjack “has richer flavour and better texture than albacore”, she says). That’s then layered with rocket, honey mustard, tasty cheese and, most importantly, a piping hot Edgell hash brown that Kim chose for its crisp outer shell. Related Article The tuna chilli sanger (with hash brown) that’s autumn’s best comfort food Then there’s the sano bread, which Kim chose after testing “countless” other brands. She won’t be drawn on where she gets it but says its “chewy but soft” texture provides the sandwich’s punctuation mark, especially when lightly toasted as it is here. Brilliant, soul-warming comfort food.

Advertisement

Milquetoast’s chip butty A British comfort classic it may be, but – all that potato! All that bread! – it’s easy for a chip butty to slip into carb-on-carb crime. But Milquetoast in the CBD have it nailed. Milquetoast’s chip butty. Markus Ravik The chefs use Tasmanian Dutch Cream potatoes sliced very thin, soaked in water, drained and then layered into a pave. The pave is baked for two hours, then pressed and cooled overnight. Then it’s cut into cubes that measure five-by-four-by-two centimetres. After all that, the bread is dead simple: Tip Top Super Thick White with the crusts removed.

Advertisement

Finally, there’s that all-important sauce – in this case, a leek aioli spiked with Taiwanese pepper salt, liquorice root, and black and white pepper. It’s slathered just thick enough inside the sandwich, with a cave-aged cheese custard on the side for dipping. Related Article ‘British people’s eyes light up’ at this luscious take on a chip butty This is the best chip butty we’ve had in Brisbane. It’s in the beautiful potato pave, which is airy and crisp but still packs that luscious texture of a Dutch cream. It’s in the silken aioli with its lovely sharpness, which acts as a through-line for the whole sandwich. And it’s in that soft bread, which couches the whole thing. Uncle Don’s katsu sando Sometimes you just want a traditional (or traditionally minded, at least) pork cutlet katsu sando. South Brisbane restaurant Uncle Don’s does that, but elevates it in all sorts of subtle ways.

Advertisement

Uncle Don’s katsu sando. Markus Ravik For the bread, Uncle Don uses a yamagata-style shokupan for its light and fluffy texture, baked locally to the restaurant’s specs. Uncle Don’s chefs then tenderise pork sourced from The Valley Butcher and bathe it in sake for a softer texture and more savouriness. Next, they bread the cutlet in room-temperature panko crumbs and let it rest before service. Related Article Find the ideal sando in this unfussy South Brisbane restaurant The pork is fried to order, layered between the shokupan with finely shredded cabbage and a housemade mayonnaise. Then, instead of a tangy tonkatsu sauce, comes the minor masterstroke: a house-made strawberry sauce, spread with the lightest of touches.

Advertisement

This thing eats so well: the bread is fresh and fluffy but never dry or too sweet, the pork is tender. There’s the crunch of the cabbage and that lovely lick of sweetness from the strawberry sauce. And it’s not too fancy. Rather, it’s what you might find at FamilyMart of 7-Eleven in Tokyo, but elevated into something that’s restaurant quality.

title: General Pants Co enters administration, putting 500 jobs at risk
text:
In brief General Pants has entered administration, putting hundreds of jobs and dozens of stores at risk.

Workers face an uncertain Christmas as administrators work to assess the retailer's future.

Hundreds of workers at collapsed fashion retailer General Pants Co face a "distressing" Christmas, and shoppers should show staff decency and sympathy, a union leader says.

General Pants has been placed into administration, leaving 500 workers and 35 stores at risk in the latest in a string of long-standing retail companies to collapse.

The youth fashion retailer, which opened in 1972 as a specialty denim store on Sydney's George Street, appointed consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal as voluntary administrators late on Wednesday.

The SDA retail union was in contact with General Pants Co and would seek discussions with the administrators, NSW secretary Bernie Smith said.

"Once again, this is a sad and distressing moment for all General Pants workers, and indeed for their colleagues across the retail sector, especially as we approach Christmas," he said.

All 35 General Pants Co stores and its online store would remain open and trade as usual, Alvarez & Marsal said in a statement.

"Customers can shop in-store and online as normal, with gift cards continuing to be accepted."

"We appeal to shoppers to treat shop floor staff with decency and sympathy at this most stressful time."

Administrators said they had taken control of the business and were working closely with the existing management team on an urgent assessment of its trading performance, stores, stock and costs.

title: Labour market 'cooling down': Australia's unemployment rate hits highest in five years
text:
In brief Australia's unemployment rate has risen to the highest level in five years.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics said there were 44,000 fewer people in employment.

Australia's unemployment rate has risen to the highest level in five years in a move that surprised many economists.

Labour force figures released on Thursday by the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed the unemployment rate rising from 4.7 per cent to 4.9 per cent for October.

It's the highest unemployment rate since the same month five years earlier.

The bureau's head of labour statistics, Sean Crick, said there were 44,000 fewer people in employment in October.

title: The Australians pushing back against a 40 million tonne emissions threat
text:
In brief Concern about data centres could shift voters in some electorates in the upcoming state election, experts say.

In September, the state Labor government laid out new rules for data centre development.

Data centre developments have emerged as a political background in the Victorian state election, with the issue having the potential to influence votes in other parts of the country as the scale of greenhouse gas emissions from the centres is revealed.

In recent months, some Victorian communities have begun mobilising against data centre projects, concerned about noise, emissions and the enormous water and energy usage they need.

The Greens have accused the Labor party of cheering on data centre progress, while experts have suggested voters may feel more aligned with candidates who oppose development, given the evidence around local sentiment.

In October, community backlash in the inner Melbourne suburb of West Footscray forced power company Jemena to pause the installation of 22-metre concrete power poles needed to supply NextDC's mammoth M3 data centre with more electricity to expand its capabilities.

NextDC chief executive Craig Scroggie later apologised to West Footscray residents about the power poles plan, saying the development would not proceed until the power issues were solved and the community and council had been consulted.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In Miners Rest, a northern suburb of Ballarat, a community group has formed in response to a Resi Ventures data centre development proposal, with organisers expressing concern about its impact on the environment, water supply, fire safety, air quality and electricity.

With Victorians now preparing to vote in the 28 November election, the issue of AI data centres could be key in some electorates.

Victorian state election

In September, the state Labor government laid out new rules for data centre development, including that they would be prohibited in residential zones and would need to be built outside a buffer zone of 150m from homes.

While asserting that data centres "support banking, healthcare, transport and emergency services" the state government said it would "set the rules" in terms of demanding data centre operators use renewable energy supplies, stay away from residential areas, and give back financially to the community.

Victorian Artificial Intelligence Minister Anthony Carbines said companies such as Amazon and Microsoft are investing in Victoria and "that will continue within sensible guardrails".

The Victorian Greens, who have zeroed in on data centres as part of their election campaign and called for a moratorium on all new developments, accused the Labor government of 'scrambling' to rein in the data centres.

"The timing of this backflip says it all. Labor spent the last year trying to turn Victoria into the data centre capital, fast-tracking projects and voting down our moratorium," Sarah Mansfield, Victorian Greens spokesperson for AI and data centres said.

"Now, weeks out from an election and just two days after the Greens led day of action in Footscray supported by hundreds of local community members, they’re scrambling to contain the political mess they created."

Dr Nathan Fioritti, a lecturer in politics from Monash University, told SBS News AI data centres have become an issue for some voters in the upcoming election, which may shift them away from the Labor government and towards parties taking a stand against them.

"Communities and electorates that are affected by this issue are looking to what others are offering. And so in Footscray, there's the Greens' offering, but also the Victorian Socialists have been quite vocal on this as part of their campaign as well. And I expect it will contribute somewhat to the seat potentially becoming winnable for the Greens," Fioritti said.

The Coalition has previously stated data centres should be built in designated precincts, while One Nation proposes banning new developments on prime agricultural land.

Community concerns

Fioritti said there are numerous concerns with data centres, but he believes a primary source of backlash is the lack of community consultation.

"I think that's probably the leading thing, not being consulted properly or not feeling like they had a say in these things without the endorsement or awareness," he said.

Evan Hamman, a research fellow at the Centre for Environmental Governance at the University of Canberra, said the consultation processes communities can participate in for data centre proposals depend on state and local planning frameworks.

READ MORE Australians' shifting attitudes towards this emerging technology revealed

He added that even when data centres pass legal processes, it doesn't necessarily mean they have community approval.

"The point to take away is that regulatory licence is not the same as social licence," Hamman said.

Ideally, Hamman believes, communities facing data centre proposals should be given adequate consultation time, objective information and the "right to get involved in a meaningful way, not a tokenistic way".

Climate Council report

Besides the issue of lack of community consultation, ongoing community concerns about data centres' environmental impacts and impacts on energy costs continue to draw attention, Fioritti said.

Without new renewables and storage to power them, Australia's data centres could push wholesale power prices up 20 per cent across the main grid by 2035, according to a new report from the Climate Council published on Thursday.

The report notes that Australia's nine "dirtiest" data centre proposals could add 40 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions a year by 2035 if they do not use renewable power.

Victoria's three data centre proposals would add 17.7 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions a year — more than Australia's highest emitting coal power station, Loy Yang A, according to the Climate Council report.

READ MORE A $3 billion downgrade could send a ripple through a surging Australian industry

In August, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced new national rules that would require data centre developers to add more renewable energy to the grid than their data centres consume, minimise water use, and ensure new sites are appropriate for their size — avoiding land that could otherwise be used for housing.

"Australia is in a strong position to attract investment in data centres, but maintaining social licence will be essential," Albanese said.

Future elections

Hamman believes data centres will likely become more of a political flashpoint in Australia in the years to come.

In the US, the overwhelming turn against Republicans in some of the party's heartland states in the recent midterm election was driven in part by opposition to data centres.

"Some of that so-called 'blue wave' was a reponse to data development and an opposition to it," Hamman said.

"What's happened internationally will eventually end up here."

As more large-scale AI data centres are proposed, Hamman believes more Australians will be moved to act on the concerns around them.

He says that newer "so-called hyperscale centres" are going to require a lot more land, a lot more water and energy, and they're going to be a lot more conspicuous in and around where people live.

title: Cameron Bancroft breaks his silence on sandpapergate saga in an explosive column
text:
In brief Cameron Bancroft supported Usman Khawaja's account of the 2018 controversy.

Bancroft said Pat Cummins' comments are at odds with what happened.

Cameron Bancroft has taken aim at Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins in an explosive column about the sandpaper scandal, insisting the whole team knew.

On the same day that Cricket Australia announced an independent forum designed as a "circuit breaker" for the game's crisis, Bancroft went into great detail about the 2018 scandal, its origins and the aftermath.

As the player who used the sandpaper on the ball, Bancroft is a central figure in the saga. He repeatedly states in the lengthy column that Usman Khawaja was right in saying that the whole team knew.

He admitted to not giving a "complete and truthful account" when questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation into what happened during the third Test against South Africa at Newlands.

Bancroft said he is angry at Cummins after his lengthy media conference last Friday, when the paceman and current Test skipper flatly denied Khawaja's claim.

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," Bancroft said in the West Australian column.

"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.

"What I saw, experienced and lived with — not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa — is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time.

"In addition to what Usman (Khawaja) already mentioned I have key recollections which affirm what he is saying."

Khawaja and Warner cast doubts on sandpapergate forum

Khawaja and David Warner said they doubt an independent forum created by Cricket Australia will heal all wounds from the sandpaper scandal.

Warner and Khawaja both questioned if the independent forum will find the truth of the controversy — and the CA hierarchy agrees.

"Someone's version of events will contradict someone else's version of events," CA chief executive Todd Greenberg told reporters in Hobart on Wednesday.

"So looking for the perfect truth doesn't exist — and we're not chasing that."

CA wants players and staffers from the infamous 2018 Test tour of South Africa, when Australia tampered with the ball, to tell their version of events to the forum.

"This forum is not about re-litigating the past," CA's interim chairman David Boon told reporters in Hobart on Wednesday.

"It's about creating an opportunity for those who wish to be heard to tell their stories in a respectful, safe environment — and for our sport to listen."

Khawaja, whose recount of the events in his autobiography released last week triggered the fresh furore, applauded CA's board for establishing the forum, but doubted its effectiveness.

"The biggest question I have is ... the board makes the decisions on what comes out at the end," Khawaja told Fox Cricket.

"How is that an actual way of trying to present what people have said? I just feel that then we just go in a circle again.

"I appreciate where their heart is and I will support the board in this ... but for me there are still a few questions."

Warner, who was banned from cricket for 12 months for his role in the sandpaper scheme, concurred.

"This safe space again — is it really going to be safe? Where do we actually end here?" he told Fox Cricket.

Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg announced the forum in Hobart. Source: AAP / James Ross

Greenberg said players and staffers from the time wouldn't be forced to attend the forum, likely to be headed by a King's Counsel and operated entirely independent of CA.

"Over the past week, we have had several different and conflicting accounts of what transpired in Cape Town in 2018," he said.

"And it has been an incredibly difficult and uncomfortable time for the game and for everyone who was involved.

"The game is really hurting at the moment.

"These events were eight years ago. They caused enormous pain and hurt for lots of people, and they're doing it again.

"And at some point we have to move forward, and we can't move forward without putting some of these steps in place."

Greenberg said CA would decide what, if any, outcome from the forum would be released publicly.

"The premise is that they (players and staff) are coming through and it's confidential," he said.

"That (outcome release) will ultimately be a matter for the CA board at the time. And, where possible, we would like to think that we can make as much of that public as we can."

There would not be sanctions for anyone involved in the forum, he said, hoping it would be completed in a month.

And Greenberg again ruled out reopening CA's investigation into the 2018 scandal completed at the time.

Eight of the 11 Australian players who played in the Cape Town Test were interviewed by that investigation, which Warner has described as a botched cover-up.

Khawaja, in his book, said the entire Test touring squad was aware of plans to tamper with the ball.

But current Test captain Pat Cummins, who was in the 2018 team, described Khawaja's claims as nonsense, while dismissing any notion of a masterplan to tamper with the ball.

CA banned Steve Smith, along with Warner, for 12 months and stripped them of the captaincy and vice-captaincy respectively for their role in the controversy.

Bancroft, who was caught by television cameras with sandpaper in his trousers during the Cape Town Test, was suspended for nine months.

title: Trump's AI push has Albanese's signature, but another country is quickly gaining ground
text:
In brief Donald Trump said he and the leaders of Australia, India and Japan are working together to "advance super intelligence".

Australia is one of several signatories to a US-led initiative aimed at securing the supply chains needed for AI development.

Technology capability and cybersecurity were prominent topics during Tuesday night's Quad meeting in the Philippines, with the leaders of Australia, the United States, Japan and India affirming support for US-led development on artificial intelligence.

In a joint press statement, the leaders said: "We are securing critical supply chains, protecting freedom of navigation and overflight, driving growth through technologies of the future including investments in and deployment of trusted Super Intelligence (SI)*".

That asterisk pointed to a clarification further down.

"*In Australia, India, and Japan, 'Super Intelligence' refers to 'artificial intelligence,'" it said.

The phrase has been a regular addition to joint statements since US President Donald Trump's executive order in September to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in all official US communications to better reflect "the full promise and opportunity of these technologies".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

AI and the resources needed for its use and development continue to shape international diplomacy, as the US and China compete for technological advancement.

Olivia Shen, the director of the strategic technologies program at the United States Studies Centre, has been to multiple Quad meetings over the years.

"Technology cooperation has always been a really important stream of work under the Quad," she told SBS News.

"So it makes sense that now we're looking at these announcements that expand on that by looking at the things that people are really worried about right now."

Key concerns include the security of undersea cables, the protection of critical mineral supply chains, and cybersecurity, particularly with advances in AI.

It's one of several disconnects developing between the view of artificial intelligence promoted by US leaders and its reception in wider society, as AI infrastructure proves divisive in communities internationally and shapes election results.

Australia signs on to US-led declaration on AI supply chain

This week, Australia, India and Japan were among 10 countries that signed a US-led declaration to strengthen controls on supply chains critical to AI development.

The San Francisco Declaration reinforces collective responsibility to protect sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure from undue influence. A spokesperson for Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the joint statement was about ensuring the technologies and supply chains Australia relied on were secure.

The agreement was part of Trump's broader Pax Silica initiative, an alliance aimed at building a global supply chain for the technology and infrastructure needed for AI among the US and allied countries. It excludes China, which has a dominant lead in producing and refining critical minerals used in AI hardware and other infrastructure.

Launched in December last year, it now has 26 signatories — including Australia, Japan and India, as well as the United Kingdom, South Korea, Singapore, and Israel.

In the Philippines, another Pax Silica signatory, the initiative has sparked protests over a proposal to build a 1,600-hectare industrial hub to support semiconductor manufacturing, the processing of critical minerals, and other AI infrastructure.

(Left to right) Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met on the sidelines of the 2026 ASEAN summit in Manila. Source: AAP / Lukas Coch

Activists opposed to the project say it will displace members of the Indigenous Aeta community and local farmers and strain water and electricity supplies.

In the capital Manila, thousands of people took part in demonstrations this week criticising Trump's arrival and — among other issues — calling for the Philippines to reject involvement in Pax Silica.

After Tuesday night's meeting, Trump said the Quad countries were working together to "advance super intelligence", which he called "the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution".

"And it's working out amazingly well," he told reporters.

Shen isn't so convinced.

"Things are not going overly well," she said.

"The reality is that US frontier models are still more advanced than Chinese rivals at this point in time, but they're about five to six months ahead of the curve."

Chinese models are gaining popularity, offering more affordable options to consumers and often released as open-weight products, enabling tweaks that let users fine-tune the model.

"The US, in a way, they're quite right that the US AI technologies win on performance and probably on security as well, considering China's past history of building in back doors and surveillance technologies into their hardware and software," Shen said.

"But I think the trend lines show that the economics of what China's offering, is getting a lot of traction."

China has also been leading its own push for collaboration through the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, which has 37 member countries, including Russia and Iran. Its signatories include 15 countries in Asia, 13 in Africa, four in Europe and five in the Americas.

"That's seen as a bit of a rival to the US-led Pax Silica initiative that is all about securing and safeguarding AI supply chains," Shen said.

"What the US is trying to offer is that countries around the world can become great by adopting the American technology stack because they have a lead over China.

"And particularly for countries that are very worried about cybersecurity and security of critical infrastructure, then they probably do want to go with the best models and they may be willing to pay a premium for it."

However, China remains excluded from access to the US' advanced chips.

Trump's government on Monday moved to close a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to train on technology from companies like Nvidia at data centres in other countries.

Some Chinese companies aren't reliant on renting US tech for training AI models so won't be affected by the crackdown but there will likely be an overall dampening on China's capabilities, Kyle Chan, a fellow in the John L Thornton China Center at The Brookings Institution, told the ABC.

He said the competition between China and the US is "very intense... but lopsided" as the US has technological advantages, while China is more focused on integrating powerful AI models into the rest of its economy.

Australia's role in the supply chain

"In terms of the bilateral relationship between Australia and the US, there is a strong sense that the US sees Australia as an important partner on critical minerals and rare earths," Shen said.

This has become more important as China has sought to restrict the access of other Quad nations over the past several years.

Rare earths are needed for electronics, semiconductors, magnets, alloys and advanced materials used in anything from data centres to jet engines.

"Rare earths are just a really important part of the supply chain where you want more diversity and we want more resilience rather than being beholden to a single source that could use that against us," Shen said.

— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press.

title: State wins carve-out from plan to make gas cheaper, but Labor still facing battle in the Senate

title: Regional house prices fall as cautious investors flee
text:
Escaping the city rat race has never looked better, with regional house prices falling as cautious investors flee.

National regional dwelling values fell 2 per cent in the past three months, almost double the rate of the previous quarter, according to market data released on Wednesday.

Queensland's regions led the decline, falling 2.7 per cent, followed by NSW at 2.1 per cent, Cotality's regional market update showed.

"Regional markets have held up better than the capitals, but they're not immune to the same pressures," the data firm's head of research Gerard Burg said.

The Gold Coast, Tweed, Bundaberg, Maryborough and Gladstone regions, which have all been hot spots for sea changers, led declines in Queensland.
