title: There might be a reason your rental has more problems, research suggests
text:
IN BRIEF Housing experts analysed national data to compare the differences in renting through an agent and a landlord.

Renters dealing with agents were more likely to report delayed repairs or unjustified rent increases.

Just a few decades ago in Australia, renting was widely seen as a stepping stone for students and young people on their way to owning a home.

Now, more Australians are renting and making rental properties a place to call home in the long term.

In many states and territories, rental laws have started to catch up, with stronger rights and protections for tenants.

Much of the debate about renting more broadly focuses on the rights of renters or the needs of landlords.

An important group is often overlooked: real estate agents and property managers.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Our new research suggests whether you rent through an agent or directly from a landlord can make a big difference.

We found tenants who were dealing with agents were more than twice as likely to say they experienced common problems.

Who manages your rental issues

Around 80 per cent of privately rented homes in Australia are rented out via agents, rather than directly from a landlord.

Agents often play a major role in renters' lives. This includes deciding who gets a property in the first place, coordinating repairs, and setting and adjusting rents.

Agents are chosen and retained by landlords. But the agent is the main, often only, person that renters can contact about their homes.

Other renters deal directly with their landlord. And the same tenancy laws apply to both arrangements. But agents and landlords who manage their own properties can have different motivations, priorities and approaches to managing a tenancy.

Agents make money from managing rental properties, not from owning them.

Given the fact it is landlords who decide whether to retain their services, the priority for agents will be keeping the business of the landlord, rather than retaining the tenant, especially in tight rental markets where vacancy rates are low.

Research in the United States has found a link between how a rental property is managed and the maintenance and security of the home.

For example, one study from Rochester, in the state of New York, found homes managed by agents were more likely to fall short of minimum housing standards than those managed by landlords.

Renting through an agent versus a landlord

So, does the same hold true in Australia? Our new research sought to find out.

Using the Australian Housing Conditions Dataset, a large-scale nationally representative survey which included over 12,000 households living in private rentals, we compared the experiences of renters renting directly from a landlord with those renting via an agent.

We compared reported renter experiences across three important aspects:

unjustified rent increases

delayed responses to maintenance requests

limitations in how the home is used — for example, restrictions on having pets or putting up pictures.

We focused on renters who had lived in their homes for at least a year and who had a formal lease agreement — excluding, for example, renting from friends or family without a formal agreement.

We found these issues were common.

Nearly one in five private renters said they had experienced an unjustified rent increase, nearly 29 per cent had experienced a restriction in how they used their home, and over one third had had a delay in repairs or maintenance.

But some renters were more likely to report these problems than others:

Source: The Conversation / Amy Clair / Sha Liu / Emma Baker

These differences remained when we adjusted for property type, household characteristics, and location.

Renters dealing with agents were 2.4 times as likely to report restrictions on how they use their homes, and 2.6 times more likely to report delayed repairs or unjustified rent increases.

Could better training and standards help?

Property agents can bring valuable expertise — including knowledge of tenancy law and systems for organising repairs.

However, as our results show, professional management does not automatically mean a better experience for renters.

Agents often manage many properties, relying on standard procedures that can leave less room for negotiation.

Renters who deal directly with landlords may have more opportunities to discuss decisions and negotiate arrangements that work for them. But some agencies discourage, even ban, direct contact between landlord and tenant.

READ MORE The Aussies who could be caught in the middle of the housing tax shake-up

For many landlords, using a property manager is convenient or necessary.

Better training for agents could improve the experience for tenants, and potentially for landlords too.

This could include skills in communicating with renters, resolving problems and understanding how management decisions affect people's ability to make a home.

Alongside clear standards and accountability, these skills could help agents meet their responsibilities to landlords while also supporting better experiences for renters.

title: Australians are the first to feel the impact of a growing global issue
text:
In Brief Two major global outages have been attributed to issues with system updates.

A popular time for system updates avoids the workday in the US and Europe, but impacts Australians instead.

Two of the biggest software outages in recent memory were caused, at least in part, by updates that went wrong. They also both set a cascade of failures in motion.

Administrators have traditionally tried to run updates during off-peak hours when people aren't online, so that if something goes wrong, the impact is minimised.

But when people all around the world working in different time zones rely on the technology, the impact is not necessarily minimised, but moved.

Last week's Microsoft outage brought emails and some calls to a stop for Australian users for nearly 24 hours and put a spotlight on how dependent the world is on a small number of global systems.

According to Dr Rahat Masood, a senior lecturer in computer science and engineering at UNSW, every company has its own rules to follow for managing updates.

"Technology companies like Microsoft, they operate globally, but their systems and updates don't always follow the same schedule everywhere," she said.

"That means a problem that might go relatively unnoticed in one country, in United States, it can cause significant disruption in another, like in Australia."

The downside of universal time

In July 2024, the CrowdStrike outage sent the world into blue-tinted chaos.

Businesses, schools, airports, supermarkets and banks around the world faced an error known as the "blue screen of death" after an issue with a cybersecurity software triggered failures in millions of Microsoft Windows devices.

At the time, the company's CEO said the issue was caused by "a defect found in a single content update".

It all started with a configuration update released at 04:09 UTC.

UTC, or Coordinated Universal Time, is the world's standard for accurately establishing clocks and time zones worldwide. It's also often used in computing and digital infrastructure to avoid ambiguity.

While similar to Greenwich Mean Time, which is still observed as a time zone in some countries, UTC doesn't operate as its own time zone, and no country officially uses it as their local time.

Passengers at airports around the world were disrupted in the CrowdStrike outage. Source: AAP / Hindustan Times/Sipa USA

The timing of CrowdStrike's update was typical.

For example, Microsoft offers a guide for managing updates using planned maintenance windows in their training materials. Their default preset for maintenance is 01:00 to 04:00. 04:00 UTC is also the start of their recommended maintenance for North and South America.

In the US, many users have already wrapped up their working days, while those in Europe are preparing for theirs, leaving neither major market predominantly online.

But in Australia, and other areas in the Asia Pacific, it's the middle of the working day.

On one side of the country, the impacts of the CrowdStrike outage hit Sydney mid-afternoon, and on the other, Perth experienced it from the middle of the day.

Based on its positioning relative to the major markets of the US and Europe, Australia's time zones are more vulnerable to being among the first to feel the impacts when updates deployed around this period go wrong.

A Sunday evening window, such as that recommended by Microsoft for systems based in the US, might avoid local users experiencing potential issues. But Australian users beginning their work week would still feel it.

A canary in the Asia Pacific?

There are two key approaches to running updates for systems used across multiple countries: choosing a single slot where the change will apply everywhere according to UTC or following the sun to gradually release as each time zone hits a certain time in their local time zone.

Unfortunately, Australia doesn't tend to fare better under either of these approaches.

Australian and New Zealand workers are among the first to log on each day, giving them access to updates before other continents wake up to begin their day. It can also make them some of the first to experience the consequences of updates gone wrong.

"When one major platform fails, either Google or Microsoft, the consequences are far beyond their borders," Masood said.

When Microsoft was unable to resolve its outage before the end of the day in the US, Australian workers woke up to begin their working day without access to their emails, messages and files.

Masood said the outage highlighted global dependence on a small number of global technology providers.

"What we have seen on Friday is that when the email was not working, when SharePoint was not working, OneDrive was not working, Teams was not working properly, we noticed that we were stopped," she said.

"Australia was not ready for this type of outage for such a long period of time and there was no alternative backups for us available."

The lack of resilience to technological failures is also a chance to support local technological production rather than tech giants.

"Can we develop something that actually we can say that this is ours and we are not dependent on the other time zones?" she said.

In the meantime, the focus should be on ensuring changes are fully tested as technology gets more complicated.

"These companies really need to think about, if they're operating globally, do it in batches, do it gradually and then go for the whole thing."

"It's better to actually make an update gradually rather than making the disruption for the whole world."

title: Investigation launched after Melbourne Cup runner dumped in skip bin
text:
IN BRIEF So You Are's trainer said he was 'deeply distressed' at the handling of the athlete's remains.

The gelding was euthanised on Monday due to a severe bout of colic.

An equine hospital has apologised to So You Are's owners and trainer after the body of the 2026 Melbourne Cup runner was left in a skip bin at a local tip.

The five-year-old gelding's dumped body was filmed at Sydney's Cleanaway Lucas Heights Resource Recovery Centre, with the graphic footage posted to social media on Monday afternoon.

His trainer Bjorn Baker confirmed on Tuesday it was So You Are, who had to be euthanised on Monday due to a severe bout of colic.

"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," the prominent conditioner said in a statement, adding he expected a full explanation of what had occurred.

"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."

Promising stayer So You Are took ill while at a spelling farm after finishing eighth in Australia's greatest race on November 3, a week after winning the Bendigo Cup.

He was rushed to REC Equine Specialists at Horsley Park in Sydney's west after showing signs of colic on Monday morning.

Surgery could not save the horse and he was euthanised under anaesthesia.

Racing NSW (RNSW) said its preliminary investigations found So You Are was being held temporarily awaiting burial when the footage was recorded.

"The way in which So You Are's body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable," the regulator said in a statement.

"So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect.

"Under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process.

"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner."

RNSW said if any wrongdoing was discovered in its ongoing investigation it would take "appropriate action".

REC Equine Specialists managing partner Jonathan Lumsden said he had spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to personally apologise.

"He should have been promptly and respectfully buried," Lumsden said.

"What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him.

"We are deeply sorry."

Lumsden pointed out the veterinary practice did not carry out the burial but acknowledged it chose the provider and arrangements, which were "not good enough" and "must change".

The practice has, effective immediately, stopped using the service provider involved and is reviewing how those it contracts care for horses after death, from collection to final burial.

Lumsden vowed to share their findings with So You Are's connections and RNSW.

"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week," Lumsden said.

"We will make sure it does not happen again."

Racing NSW is also reviewing its existing rules and minimum standards and has promised to work with the Department of Primary Industries on steps to avoid a repeat.

Baker added his thoughts remained with So You Are's owner-breeder Stuart Ramsey and family and with all the stable's staff, "for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss".

title: What we know about the planned Rwanda migrant deportation centre
text:
In brief The initiative was taken by Austria, Germany, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands.

Nationals of any country are eligible, according to those involved in the plan.

Five European Union (EU) countries overnight announced a plan to establish a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda, the first such facility outside the bloc.

Here is what we know about the "return-hub" initiative by Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands.

Who will be deported and how?

The five nations have been exploring sending migrants to centres outside Europe for months, with the pilot project planned to be launched next year.

During a joint press announcement in Vienna, ministers from the five EU countries and Rwanda remained evasive on the project's scope.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But according to people involved, the centre will house around 100 migrants.

They will be men and women whose asylum applications have been rejected but who refuse to return to their countries of origin, despite having exhausted all avenues of appeal.

According to those involved in the plan, nationals of any country will be eligible to be sent to the facility, although minors would be excluded.

National authorities from the five European countries' national authorities will be responsible for transferring rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

Non-governmental refugee and humanitarian organisations are worried the initiative could ultimately target all asylum seekers — a claim denied by the five countries involved.

What conditions will migrants face in Rwanda?

Once they arrive in Rwanda, authorities of the east African country will take charge of them, and they will receive residence permits.

They will be placed in a centre, which Rwandan authorities referred to as a "welcome centre".

The five European countries insist that it will be open, without any deprivation of liberty or barbed wire.

READ MORE Tony Burke announces backpacker visa backdown after industry pressure

A site has already been identified. The European countries, however, have refused to specify where it is.

They only stress that it is not one of the centres the United Kingdom had planned to use.

London had announced plans in 2022 to send asylum seekers to Rwanda, but the project was ultimately abandoned because of legal obstacles.

How long will the migrants stay at the centre?

The idea is for the migrants to stay in the centre for a few months, with the aim that they then integrate into Rwandan society.

"These illegal migrants who will be relocated to Rwanda are not going to be kept in a camp or in a dedicated area. They will be integrated in our society," Rwandan interior minister Vincent Biruta told the press conference in Vienna.

Vocational training and language courses are to be offered to them.

The five EU countries also say an independent monitoring mechanism — the details of which have not been spelled out — will be put in place to ensure respect for human rights.

Another option is for the exiles to return voluntarily to their country of origin, but not to the EU.

Is the move legal?

Those involved in the plan hope it will discourage migrants from trying to settle on the European continent, besides getting those asylum seekers whose applications have been rejected out of the EU.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the project aimed to send a "signal ... that you can no longer enter the European Union illegally and think that you can just stay around".

The EU states have refused to say what Rwanda would receive in return.

The five countries claim that the legal basis is solid, relying on relevant EU legislation adopted a few months ago.

They have dismissed fierce criticism and concern about the treatment of migrants.

The plans are expected to face court challenges.

Deputy legislative council president Steve Martin has taken the extraordinary step of clearing the public gallery following outbursts from WA Greens supporters during a debate over proposed legislation to ban forest mining. WA Greens MLC Jess Beckerling on Thursday proposed an amendment to the Mining Act 1978 and called for a ban to native forest mining. More than 100 supporters were removed from the public gallery at Parliament House on Thursday. “There are some places in the world that are off limits to mining and native forests belong up the top of that list,” she told parliament. “I know there are many individual members in this place that know this, and it is time for it to be put into law.”

The proposed bill aims to amend the Mining Act 1978 so native forest land could not be the subject of a mining tenement, and to ban clearing of native forest vegetation for mining purposes. It is aimed almost directly at US alumina giant Alcoa, which mines the state’s northern jarrah forest extensively for bauxite. Following the introduction of the bill, WA Greens leader Brad Pettit made a motion without notice calling on the state government to align its actions to the seriousness of the climate emergency by, in addition to banning forest mining, also banning new fossil fuel projects and implementing a fossil fuel phase out plan. However, during a response to the motion, opposition MP Steve Thomas, who referred to himself as “the Liberal who believes in climate change”, was interrupted several times by viewers in the public gallery. Following the first interruption, Thomas told the more than 100 members of the public: “Unfortunately you are only embarrassing yourselves.”

The Australian sharemarket’s losing streak continued on Thursday, with the local bourse falling for a sixth straight session and wiping out the rest of this year’s gains as global AI anxiety weighed on the mining and tech sectors and Australia reported its highest unemployment rate since 2021. The S&P/ASX 200 closed 91.40 points, or 1 per cent, lower at 8730.40, basically flat from its level at the start of the year. Mining heavyweights led the losses after the price of copper, seen as integral to the AI boom, plunged by almost 6 per cent overnight. The Australian dollar slid 0.5 per cent to $US66.86¢, also wiping out its gains for the year, on the back of the weak employment data. Global markets are on an unsteady footing as doubts over AI companies hover. AP The newly created AFR Real Economy index – which tracks 500 companies that mirror the ABS’ composition of the actual economy– was down 0.5 per cent, while the AFR Global 50, which tracks Australia’s top 50 companies with majority revenue from offshore, slumped 1.4 per cent. The Australian Bureau of Statistics’ labour force data showed the Reserve Bank’s aggressive tightening of monetary policy has hit the jobs market, with the unemployment rate spiking to 4.9 per cent last month. Unemployment rose by 0.2 percentage points, reaching its highest level since 2021.

The weaker-than-expected labour market reinforced bets that the RBA has ended its interest-rate hike cycle and will pivot to cuts next year, sending the Aussie dollar to its lowest since early January. Related Article Analysis

Interest rates One foot in recession: The unemployment numbers that blow up the RBA’s case for hikes “This release all but closes the door on a December hike and shifts the debate to how long rates stay at their peak,” said Sunny Nguyen, head of the Australian economics team at Moody’s Analytics. While prospects of an interest rate reprieve usually boost sentiment, it wasn’t enough to dispel dark clouds over the AI trade, which has been driving global markets this year and is faltering amid fears the heavily indebted and interdependent sector could also make them crash. Despite those concerns, AI frontier lab Anthropic – the company behind chatbot Claude – released the pricing for its Wall Street float. Bloomberg said the stock will be set at $US83 per share, above its target range of $US70 to $US78, valuing the company at $US1.5 trillion ($2.2 trillion). The company is set to start trading on Friday morning (AEDT).

Mining stocks plunged yet again on the ASX, with BHP down another 3.7 per cent and Rio Tinto down 4.1 per cent. Copper steadied after plunging almost 6 per cent overnight – the biggest drop since April 2025 – on a sharp unwinding of bullish bets tied to AI and US tariffs. The red metal has lost 12 per cent so far in November, fuelled by growing doubts over the durability of AI-related spending and fading expectations for US tariffs on refined copper. Anthropic investors are undeterred Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Gold miners also extended losses, with Northern Star slumping 5.7 per cent, Evolution Mining plunging 7.3 per cent and Newmont down 4.6 per cent. Gold wavered near a 14-month low after Federal Reserve officials signalled its interest-rate hikes are likely to stretch into next year, making the non-yielding metal less attractive for investors. Financial stocks were holding up better, with Commonwealth Bank up 0.4 per cent, while Westpac dropped 0.2 per cent, ANZ Bank slipped 0.1 per cent and National Australia Bank dropped 0.9 per cent. Energy stocks finished lower, with Woodside Energy down 2 per cent, Santos down 1.9 per cent and refiner Ampol down 2.7 per cent. Oil had slumped overnight, but steadied as traders assessed the outlook for the US-Iran conflict, including the possibility of fresh attacks against Tehran, with Brent holding above $US92 a barrel. US President Donald Trump is weighing plans for further strikes, the New York Times reported, citing US and Israeli officials. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing him to join a four- to seven-day campaign, it said.

The question is whether Nvidia’s big growth can continue despite the turmoil created by the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. “Whoever tells the story first controls the narrative,” writes Sofia Franklyn in Daddy Issues, her memoir detailing her own side of her spectacular exit from the hit podcast Call Her Daddy. For Franklyn, it’s a hard-won insight. It’s widely known as the “biggest podcast fumble in history” – Franklyn ostensibly bungling herself out of a deal that her one-time partner, Alex Cooper, has spun into a $US500 million media and lifestyle empire, the Unwell Network. Franklyn has been on the losing end of the public narrative ever since. Sofia Franklyn’s memoir Daddy Issues is best described as revenge served ice-cold. The fallout was initially framed by Cooper, who in 2020 posted a slick video telling the podcast’s #DaddyGang fans that Franklyn’s greed, laziness and subservience to a man (her boyfriend at the time, HBO executive Peter Nelson, the book’s tragic collateral damage) were to blame for their split. It was then cemented by the pair’s original boss, Barstool Sports kingpin Dave Portnoy, who framed Franklyn as a messy, entitled brat in his tacky memoir (please, let us never speak of it again), Cancel Me If You Can. Franklyn’s late entry – revenge served ice-cold – spins another perspective to the saga, detailing Cooper’s behind-the-scenes backstabbing and calculated manoeuvring. She frames Cooper as a Gatsby-meets-Brutus character: secretive, unreliable, a ruthless social climber who’d mysteriously cut ties with her past.

Advertisement

Of course, it was all good at first. Early scenes highlight their sisterly (almost sapphic, Franklyn implies) camaraderie as Manhattan transplants. Later chapters drop in digs that explain the book’s opening revelation that Cooper’s husband, Matt Kaplan, called Franklyn’s publisher saying Cooper was threatening to sue before the book was even written. “It’s the first I’ve heard from Alex in six years. The first since the fallout, when she stopped responding to my text messages,” writes Franklyn. The icky, enticing dirty laundry is worth the price of admission. And Franklyn is such a thoughtful and emotive writer, naturally comfortable with contradictions, that even those not so invested in this Rashomon for the world of obnoxious Millennial podcasting will be adding Daddy Issues to the great canon of messy memoirs, alongside Elizabeth Wurtzel’s Prozac Nation, Cat Marnell’s How to Murder Your Life and Julia Fox’s Down the Drain. Look, I’m surprised, too. Starting from her wild childhood (drinking, drugs, sex, jail time), Franklyn deftly underscores why the betrayal hit so hard. Sure, $200 million is probably most of it, but it also comes down to the ravaging of a belief she held sacred: that in a world of horrible men, women always had her back. Call Her Daddy’s Alex Cooper and husband Matt Kaplan. Getty Images for Netflix Growing up, the male presence in Franklyn’s life was either negligible or volatile. Her mother, an Argentinian immigrant who worked at a DV shelter, had her young. Her biological father, a Spanish man named Joaquin, was entirely absent. Her stepfather, Tom, a New Zealander, struggled with drug abuse. Elsewhere, her experiences with men have been violent or criminal.

Advertisement

The stalwarts in her life, unconditionally supportive, have been women: her mum, her grandma, her mum’s sisters and Spanish friends, her childhood friend Mia. It’s why, when the Call Her Daddy shit hits the fan, it’s unfathomable to Franklyn that another woman would do this to her. Photo: As she herself writes, Franklyn’s smarts have been underestimated due to her now trademark vocal fry (listen to the audiobook, it’s worth it). Her sharp imagery puts you in the centre of her paranoid spiral, to the point where she’s accusing her own mum of spying on her. A scene where she’s begging Cooper to let her back on the show, realising she has no alternative path, is gruesome. Another, where she’s reacting in real-time to Cooper’s viral “The Truth About Call Her Daddy” video, is devastating. “Lost a friend? I’m right here. Just answer my texts. I’m waving the white flag,” she writes. By the book’s end, after her desperation is exhausted – like all good writers, Franklyn has no censor when it comes to depicting herself at her most pitiful and depraved – that white flag takes on new symbolism: a clean slate. When Franklyn – broken and literally unwell in a pharmacy where she’s shopping for medicine – comes across Cooper’s signature on a hydration drink, she laughs at the cosmic absurdity.

Advertisement

Much of the book, like that scene, plays like a parting shot at whatever remains of Call Her Daddy’s #girlboss-era feminism (an easier stance to take when you didn’t land the bag). It’s also bait from someone so unscrupulously written out of the main story: Alex Cooper will surely have to re-engage at some point, which you imagine is all Sofia Franklyn ever wanted. It’s the saga we need and deserve. Daddy Issues by Sofia Franklyn is published by Simon and Schuster ($37). The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. title: ‘She believed it was wrong’: The team staffer who spoke up against sandpaper
text:

SportCricketBall tampering ‘She believed it was wrong’: The team staffer who spoke up against sandpaper Chris Barrett Updated November 19, 2026 — 5:03pm ,first published 2:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In the week before the third Test at Newlands in 2018, Australian team media manager Kate Hutchison dropped her own bombshell. Over lunch in Stellenbosch, a famed wine region just east of Cape Town, she told reporters covering the series that she was resigning after six years with Cricket Australia. Loading She was leaving not as a result of the Australian team’s use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball, which we now know had been going on since the previous match in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha. Instead, she had tired of their out-of-control behaviour, which had spiralled in South Africa, and of the demands of being on the road for more than half the year.

Advertisement

Eight years later, Hutchison has been cast by Cameron Bancroft as the lone voice of dissent against Australia’s ploy to cheat on the tour by using sandpaper to rough up one side of the ball. In a blow-by-blow account of the scandal that has propelled CA and the Test captaincy of Pat Cummins into crisis, the former opener describes Hutchison “expressing her objection to what was happening” in a team huddle on the morning of day three in Gqeberha. Kate Hutchison with then-captain Steve Smith at Adelaide Oval in 2017. Ryan Pierse His use of sandpaper late on day two was being discussed in the group at the time, Bancroft said. “I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion,” he said of Hutchison.

Advertisement

“I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up. Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it.” Bancroft also referred to a conversation with Hutchison at training before the next Test in Cape Town, where he was caught with sandpaper on the field. Loading “I asked what would happen if I was caught tampering with the ball. She did not want to engage in that conversation because of the seriousness of the consequences, but her response was, ‘Not good’, and she walked off,” he said. Hutchison, who went on to work for Swimming Australia and the AFL and is now head of corporate communications for the RACV, declined to comment on Thursday.

Advertisement

Sources who spoke on the condition of anonymity said she has no dispute with Bancroft’s account but is uncomfortable being presented as a moral compass of some kind after the fact. Like most media managers, she has no desire to be the story herself. A straight shooter, it comes as little surprise to those who know Hutchison that she would have spoken up about what she thought. Kate Hutchison (right) with swimmer Ariarne Titmus at the Australian Open last year. Getty Images As a media professional, her role didn’t involve being present when the team was devising or discussing tactics. But she would have been acutely aware that such brazen manipulation of the ball could backfire publicly if it was exposed, although even she could not have anticipated the extent of the fallout and for how long it would endure.

Advertisement

Hutchison, like many in the 30-plus touring party in South Africa of players, coaches and staff, has wrestled with the events of 2018 while abiding by an effective omertà in the years since, according to the same sources. A New Zealander who joined CA in 2012 and handled media duties for an Australian under-19s tour and a women’s World Cup before joining the men’s team set-up, she had come under intense scrutiny at the time over the notorious press conference at Newlands in which Bancroft and Steve Smith lied. Darren Lehmann (right) and bowling coach David Saker have been drawn into the scandal by Cameron Bancroft. AP Their dishonesty dug them into a deeper hole and was such a disaster that one leading television newsman said the media manager should be sacked. However, it had long been suggested that Smith had been advised not to go to the press conference that day while in such an emotional state, and Usman Khawaja confirmed in his autobiography that he and Hutchison had tried to talk the captain out of it.

Advertisement

Related Article Ball tampering Lehmann dodges question on Bancroft claims, leaves commentary box When it became clear that there was no changing Smith’s mind, it’s understood she was among those who urged him and Bancroft not to lie. This masthead revealed last week that bowling coach David Saker had allegedly told them “You can’t say sandpaper”, and Bancroft recalls Saker “specifically warning against identifying sandpaper as the material used”. The fact that they followed that advice – and overlooked the counsel of others – is evidence of the culture of denial and the toxic bubble that existed around the team under the control of head coach Darren Lehmann. Bancroft said he “cannot speak for Kate’s thoughts beyond what I remember her saying and doing” and that “she deserves the opportunity to give her own account”. Having well and truly moved on from her stint with cricket, Hutchison has no intention of doing that.

title: The best Brisbane sandwiches of the past 12 months
text:
Advertisement

Eating outSandwich Watch The best Brisbane sandwiches of the past 12 months From a Hainanese chicken sandwich and a fancy chip butty, to one made with pizza dough, these are the past year’s essential sangers. Matt Shea November 19, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

We joked last year that we should rename Sandwich Watch to Sandwich Search, such is the number of dragons you sometimes need to slay to get to the royalty around town. But we also said a rising tide lifts all boats, and that really rung true when reflecting on what we ate between two slices of bread in the past 12 months. The quality has definitely stepped up around Brisbane, as the bogus recommendations stepped off. Uncle Don makes a contender for the city’s best katsu sando. Markus Ravik October ticked off this column’s second anniversary. To mark the milestone, here are the best sandwiches we’ve eaten in the past 12 months. Jane’s Deli’s Hainanese chicken sandwich

Advertisement

Why hasn’t someone thought of this before? Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Jane’s Deli Hainanese chicken sandwich is one of the best in town. Markus Ravik Hainanese chicken is, of course, usually associated with chicken rice, a national dish in Singapore (alongside chilli crab) that’s also enormously popular in neighbouring Malaysia. One caveat about sticking it in a sandwich, though, is that much of the flavour of chicken rice often comes from the rice and typical condiments such as spicy garlic chilli, dark soy and ginger sauce. But Jane’s owners and chefs Jianne Jeong and Leaham Claydon have this covered. Related Article Brisbane’s best sanger? This Hainanese chicken number is a contender

Advertisement

Let’s start with that bread. It’s a pain de mie, the silky, fluffy French-style sandwich loaf characterised by its soft interior and thin crust, which will reaffirm your faith in the humble white-bread sanger. The pain de mie is given a liberal smear of mayonnaise, a layer of salted cucumber, and shredded iceberg. For the protein, whole chickens are hot brined with shaoxing, ginger and spring onions. The resulting bird is juicy but firm, and the skin has been left on, again recalling a traditional chicken rice. The final flourish is a drizzle of Mama Liu’s chilli oil (which is on the shelves at Jane’s Deli) for a big dash of umami. Related Article Brisbane’s best sandwiches? Here are our top picks of the past year We bang on in this column sometimes about chef-made sandwiches, but this is absolutely that, with a clear, purposeful flavour profile. Please go eat it. Olli Italiano’s mortadella panuozzo

Advertisement

Like so many great sandwiches, the beauty of Olli Italiano’s mortadella panuozzo’s (a “pizza sandwich”) lies in its simplicity. The mortadella, supplied by Selecta Food Group, is made by an Italian family in Melbourne. This is complemented with a fistful of springy rocket, gooey stracciatella from Byron Bay Mozzarella, and a liberal sprinkle of pistachio – as much for texture as it is flavour. Olli Italiano’s Panuozzo are huge, and therefore excellent value. Morgan Roberts Simple, except it’s wrapped inside an almighty pizza base made with Italian 00 flour, filled with fior di latte and cooked fast at 350 degrees in this East Brisbane restaurant’s drop-door pizza oven to produce a bubbly, crispy Neapolitan-ish crust. It’s then finished with a generous sprinkle of pecorino for a bit of seasoning. And that’s it. Related Article You need to eat this mortadella pizza sanger that’s as big as your face

Advertisement

It makes for a luscious, deeply satisfying sandwich that’s as big as your face, yet easy to eat with one hand (after the chefs cut it in two, at least). Anytime Coffee’s deli sandwich Anytime Coffee’s sandwiches have always been at least pretty good, but it was its brilliant deli sandwich that registered with this column recently. Anytime’s deli sandwich. Markus Ravik Deli sandwiches require precision and Anytime’s take is about as precise as it gets – which is impressive when you discover how much is going on under the hood. For meats, Anytime uses leg ham, salami cotto and capocollo sourced from Rayner’s Meats in New Farm. That’s layered with crunchy rocket, pickled red onion, and a green olive and guindilla mix that’s arguably the sandwich’s secret weapon.

Advertisement

Sealing it all off is some provolone dolce. It’s there for its creamy texture and to protect the bread, which is why the Anytime crew has opted for a milder take on the semi-hard Italian cheese. Related Article Finally, the deli sandwich we’ve been searching for in Brisbane Talking bread, all this is squeezed between two slices of a light-rye sourdough tin loaf that’s produced by NYC Bagel for Anytime from a Riser Bread recipe. If not the perfect deli sandwich, it’s pretty damn close. Nali Kitchen’s braised beef brisket sandwich

Advertisement

Imagine the messy hot roast beef sandwich from the corner carvery of your youth, but given the best kind of glow-up. Nali Kitchen's braised brisket sandwich recalls the corner carvery beef sanger of your youth. Markus Ravik That’s the approach at Nali Kitchen in Gresham Lane in the CBD. Here, the brisket is braised rather than smoked (“we are not a smokehouse and don’t try to be”, owner and chef Matthew Van Der Zwan says), left overnight in a stock that’s kept “pretty muted” to help let the quality of the protein shine through. Van Der Zwan prefers Riverina Angus rump cap. Cleverly, the accompaniments across all of Nali Kitchen’s sandwiches are the same – charred onion, rocket, salsa verde and aioli – keeping the focus squarely on the quality of the meat. Everything is then slapped between two slices of focaccia that are soft enough to soak up any decadence that might try to slip out. Related Article Introducing the roast beef sanger of your dreams

Advertisement

Brisket is a relatively heavy cut of beef, partly because of the connective collagen that holds the muscles together, and partly because of its inherently high fat content. But the 16-hour braise leaves it juicy and tender, and the rocket and salsa verde give it a lovely herbaceous lift. The whole thing is then tied together by the sweet, nutty aioli, and it eats like a dream. Sunny Side Sandwiches’ eggplant offering Sunny Side Sandwiches has evolved over the years. The menu has expanded, then been reduced. Certain menu items have come, then gone again. Sunny Side Sandwiches’ eggplant offering. Morgan Roberts But according to co-owner Mack Bowers, there’s one that hasn’t changed – the eggplant sandwich.

Advertisement

It’s a variation on the triple-store setup’s star chicken schnitty sandwich, using the same chopped iceberg lettuce dressed in Japanese mayo, dill, parsley and chives; the same bread and butter pickles; the same shokupan bread; and then a “magic sprinkle” of the same signature seasoning, which features salt, nutritional yeast, Korean chilli flakes, and “a few other little secret herbs and spices”. In the middle, though, instead of chook there are two slices of eggplant that have been bathed in saltwater, panko crumbed, then stored in the freezer to help them set before being tossed in the frier. Related Article Brisbane’s best vegetarian sanger? This glorious thing is a contender The result is a contender for Brisbane’s best vegetarian sandwich. There’s the crispness of the eggplant, the crunch of the iceberg, the acid of the pickles, the velvety texture of the mayo with its tangy stack of herbs. And then there’s the deep, deep umami of the “magic sprinkle”. Still, for us, the shokupan is the real star here. It’s baked in-house, meaning it’s ultra-consistent and able to be sliced thinly while maintaining its integrity.

Advertisement

Naldham Terrace’s French beef baguette with dipping sauce There are a lot of great sandwiches around town at the moment, but not so many great French dips, where roast beef is stuffed into a crusty French baguette and served with a broth on the side. Until now, that is. Naldham Terrace’s French beef baguette with dipping sauce (beer optional). Markus Ravik Introducing, the Naldham Terrace French beef baguette with dipping sauce. Served outside on the ground floor at the greenery-lined Naldham House, it’s one of the best sandwiches you can get in the CBD. There’s almost nothing to this sanger: a baguette, some steak, caramelised onions and seeded mustard. But also, that’s selling it short.

Advertisement

The baguette is a tight little number baked daily by Eustralis, a specialist European food supplier, that’s been crisped just so for serving. The steak is a generous stack of S. Kidman two-to-three score flank, cooked medium rare and basted in the pan in butter, garlic and thyme. And the seeded mustard is Covinor, a quality French brand. Related Article This classy French steak sanga comes with a luscious dipping broth The Naldham chefs have nailed pulling it all together. There’s the crisp crunch of the baguette, the maillard, and the juiciness of the grilled flank, the sweetness from the caramelised onion, and the tangy vinegar of the mustard. Then there’s the side of broth, which is a heavenly bowl of stocky goodness. It has the right consistency to coat the sandwich without overpowering what’s slapped inside. And it’s dead simple to eat. Baguette sangers can get unwieldy but this is easy to manage, and the flank is tender enough that you won’t return to the office looking like you’ve been in a food fight.

Advertisement

Lindy’s Po Boys’ shrimp po’ boy Originating in New Orleans in 1929 as a cheap (or free) meal for striking streetcar workers, a po’ boy is similar to a submarine sandwich but defined by a more French-leaning roll that’s similar to a traditional baguette but lighter and fluffier inside. Lindy’s Po Boys’ shrimp po’ boy. Markus Ravik Typical fillings are prawns (shrimp, of course, in US parlance), roast beef and Louisiana hot sausage, and a traditional sandwich might be “dressed” with lettuce, tomato, pickles and mayonnaise. Steve Lind fell in love with po’ boys when travelling as a musician in 2016 and Lindy’s Po Boys was eventually born earlier this year. This column caught it on its third pop-up at Camp Hill Bowls Club.

Advertisement

On the menu was a pork sausage po’ boy and a shrimp po’ boy. It’s the latter we think you need to eat ASAP. The bread is made to Lind’s specs by Norman Park’s Golden K Bakery. It’s crisp on the outside (without being banh mi crunchy) and soft and pillowy on the inside – tasty, textural, moreish. Related Article This shrimp po’ boy is the perfect Brisbane sandwich. Here’s why For the dressing, Lind uses a moderate amount of iceberg lettuce, a few slices of tomato, and Fehlbergs burger pickles. He then gives each bun a squirt of Hellmann’s mayonnaise, Heinz tomato sauce, and Louisiana Hot Sauce for “acidity and sweetness”. For prawns, there’s nothing fancy, with Lind opting for wild-caught prawns from the supermarket so he can pile plenty of them into the sandwich. The batter, though, is special – a combination of plain flour, corn starch, and then cornflour for a dash of extra colour.

Advertisement

The result has all that texture from the fried prawns (which remain juicy inside), crispy iceberg and precision baked bread, but then stacks of acid, and salt and sweetness from the dressings and sauces. Also, unlike a banh mi or other baguette-based sandwiches, it’s a cinch to eat. We’ll keep you posted about the next pop-up. Sincerity by Jacorey’s chilli tuna mayo sandwich What initially attracted us to this brilliant sandwich was – counterintuitively, perhaps – its relative practicality when compared to its more Instagrammable stablemates at Upper Mt Gravatt’s Sincerity by Jacorey (the ebi katsu, in particular, is a real peacock of a sanger). Sincerity by Jacorey’s chilli tuna mayo sandwich. Markus Ravik

Advertisement

It might sound like a spicy tuna toastie but it’s much more than that. Co-owner Jamie Kim mixes skipjack tuna with kewpie mayo and a bunch of spices to create the silky chilli tuna mix at the heart of the sandwich (Skipjack “has richer flavour and better texture than albacore”, she says). That’s then layered with rocket, honey mustard, tasty cheese and, most importantly, a piping hot Edgell hash brown that Kim chose for its crisp outer shell. Related Article The tuna chilli sanger (with hash brown) that’s autumn’s best comfort food Then there’s the sano bread, which Kim chose after testing “countless” other brands. She won’t be drawn on where she gets it but says its “chewy but soft” texture provides the sandwich’s punctuation mark, especially when lightly toasted as it is here. Brilliant, soul-warming comfort food.

Advertisement

Milquetoast’s chip butty A British comfort classic it may be, but – all that potato! All that bread! – it’s easy for a chip butty to slip into carb-on-carb crime. But Milquetoast in the CBD have it nailed. Milquetoast’s chip butty. Markus Ravik The chefs use Tasmanian Dutch Cream potatoes sliced very thin, soaked in water, drained and then layered into a pave. The pave is baked for two hours, then pressed and cooled overnight. Then it’s cut into cubes that measure five-by-four-by-two centimetres. After all that, the bread is dead simple: Tip Top Super Thick White with the crusts removed.

Advertisement

Finally, there’s that all-important sauce – in this case, a leek aioli spiked with Taiwanese pepper salt, liquorice root, and black and white pepper. It’s slathered just thick enough inside the sandwich, with a cave-aged cheese custard on the side for dipping. Related Article ‘British people’s eyes light up’ at this luscious take on a chip butty This is the best chip butty we’ve had in Brisbane. It’s in the beautiful potato pave, which is airy and crisp but still packs that luscious texture of a Dutch cream. It’s in the silken aioli with its lovely sharpness, which acts as a through-line for the whole sandwich. And it’s in that soft bread, which couches the whole thing. Uncle Don’s katsu sando Sometimes you just want a traditional (or traditionally minded, at least) pork cutlet katsu sando. South Brisbane restaurant Uncle Don’s does that, but elevates it in all sorts of subtle ways.

Advertisement

Uncle Don’s katsu sando. Markus Ravik For the bread, Uncle Don uses a yamagata-style shokupan for its light and fluffy texture, baked locally to the restaurant’s specs. Uncle Don’s chefs then tenderise pork sourced from The Valley Butcher and bathe it in sake for a softer texture and more savouriness. Next, they bread the cutlet in room-temperature panko crumbs and let it rest before service. Related Article Find the ideal sando in this unfussy South Brisbane restaurant The pork is fried to order, layered between the shokupan with finely shredded cabbage and a housemade mayonnaise. Then, instead of a tangy tonkatsu sauce, comes the minor masterstroke: a house-made strawberry sauce, spread with the lightest of touches.

Advertisement

This thing eats so well: the bread is fresh and fluffy but never dry or too sweet, the pork is tender. There’s the crunch of the cabbage and that lovely lick of sweetness from the strawberry sauce. And it’s not too fancy. Rather, it’s what you might find at FamilyMart of 7-Eleven in Tokyo, but elevated into something that’s restaurant quality.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
